articles.title: Small-scale projects offer hope for Gaza farmers rebuilding lives
articles.excerpt: Nuseirat, Gaza Strip – Mohammad al-Halabi, 50, bends over tomato and eggplant seedlings in a 300-square-metre plot in the middle of central Gaza’s Nuseirat refugee camp, inspecting the leaves, waterin...
articles.body_text:
Nuseirat, Gaza Strip – Mohammad al-Halabi, 50, bends over tomato and eggplant seedlings in a 300-square-metre plot in the middle of central Gaza’s Nuseirat refugee camp, inspecting the leaves, watering the plants and monitoring their growth.

The small plot he is tending is an attempt to reclaim his old profession as a farmer with his father, Marwan, on their land in northern Gaza’s Jabalia.

Al-Halabi once owned a much bigger plot of farmland – around 40,000 square metres (about 10 acres) – in northern Gaza, where he grew strawberries, tomatoes, flowers, potatoes and eggplants. His four children – Mahmoud, 30, Reham, 27, Issa, 24, and Omar, 20 – also worked with him and relied on farming as a source of income for the family.

“I have been working in agriculture since I was a child,” al-Halabi said. “The land is my life, and I have spent my whole life farming it.”

Al-Halabi says his entire farmland was bulldozed in February 2024 by Israeli forces, as part of their general destruction of Jabalia. Al-Halabi’s land there is now covered with rubble and remnants of war, including what he described as remnants of missiles and other weapons.

He believes it will require extensive rehabilitation work before it can be farmed again.

So, for now, al-Halabi’s focus is on his small plot in Nuseirat, which he began renting at the start of the war, after his displacement. He began growing whatever he could obtain.

“Agriculture is my profession,” al-Halabi said. “Even after being displaced, I couldn’t leave it. I found a small piece of land and planted whatever I could get.”

The plot produces only a few kilogrammes of each crop he grows, barely enough for his family, and is too small to generate enough produce for sale.

“When I see the plant growing and producing a fruit, I feel that I can still farm,” al-Halabi said. “The land is small, but it has potential, and hopefully it will produce a crop.”

Data from Gaza’s Government Media Office illustrates the scale of the damage to the agricultural sector.

More than 87 percent of Gaza’s agricultural land has been destroyed. About 8,700 agricultural wells have also been destroyed and put out of service, while 7,748 cattle, sheep and poultry farms have been destroyed. More than 87 percent of greenhouses have also been damaged. Annual vegetable and fruit production has fallen from about 524,000 tonnes to approximately 20,000.

Naser Deeb, director-general of the Agricultural Extension at Gaza’s Ministry of Agriculture, says the damage extends beyond crops to farmland, water sources, irrigation networks, wells and agricultural facilities. Deeb says he has visited and assessed several damaged agricultural sites across Gaza, though he did not inspect al-Halabi’s land.

Deeb said damaged farmland would need extensive rehabilitation before production could resume.

“Farmers today are facing several problems at the same time,” Deeb says. “Even if a farmer returns to his land, that does not mean the land is ready for cultivation. The soil needs to be rehabilitated, water sources and irrigation systems repaired, and seeds, fertilisers and equipment provided.”

And the impact of these issues, Deeb says, is affecting farming families and markets across Gaza, reducing the availability of fresh vegetables and making it harder for farmers to restore their livelihoods.

Some farmers are trying to rebuild through small-scale projects.

Mohammad Abdul Naser Hassan al-Jadba, 40, from Sheikh Ajleen in Gaza City, lost his source of income during the war after his farmland ended up on the wrong side of the “Yellow Line”, the boundary in Gaza behind which Israeli forces operate and control.

Israeli soldiers have killed Palestinians who have strayed too close to the line, and al-Jadba knows that it is too dangerous for him to even try to access his farmland. Instead, he resigned himself to renting a small plot in Deir el-Balah, where he has established a nursery and greenhouse to grow tomatoes, eggplants and peppers.

Al-Jadba received some funding from a Belgian development fund, which he used to build the greenhouse and obtain agricultural supplies.

“Before renting the farm, my income was zero,” al-Jadba said. “Today, I can support my family, and my monthly income has reached around 3,000 shekels [$1,015] a month.”

He has also been able to employ two farmers on a permanent basis inside the greenhouse. Both had previously been unemployed.

“For me, this project was not just agricultural support,” al-Jadba said. “It was a real opportunity to return to work, regain my source of income and become self-reliant again.”

articles.title: Westminster council threatens Charing Cross soup kitchen with closure
articles.excerpt:
Conservative authority says site is not safe for vulnerable people charity serves or general public

Westminster council is making it “impossible” for soup kitchens to operate by complaining about the...
articles.body_text:
Conservative authority says site is not safe for vulnerable people charity serves or general public

Westminster council is making it “impossible” for soup kitchens to operate by complaining about the “crowds of vulnerable people” who turn up to be fed, a charity has said.

Steven Stuart, who founded Friends of Essex & London Homeless (FOELH) with his wife, Cheryl, a decade ago, said constant complaints from the council could force the soup kitchen to shut down.

The council is also facing a licensing battle with the London mayor, Sadiq Khan, who has objected to its restrictive new draft policy that would ban new bars and pubs from opening in Soho and the West End. The council also plans to restrict “vertical drinking” – standing while having a pint – in new bars, pubs and restaurants.

The homeless charity runs a weekly event in Charing Cross, where volunteers hand out hot meals. It also provides new clothes and sleeping bags to rough sleepers, and runs a food bank.

But Westminster council has sent enforcement agents to the soup kitchen, warning that it cannot operate as it currently does and raising concerns about noise and litter.

Phil Jones, a FOELH volunteer, said: “We’ve received notice from the council that they intend to ban us from operating our weekly soup kitchen in Charing Cross. They cite litter issues but we clear away all waste and leave the area spotless, so that’s just an excuse from them.”

Stuart said: “We are facing increasing challenges with Westminster city council surrounding our weekly Charing Cross outreach. Various requirements and obstacles are making it increasingly difficult to provide the consistent support that vulnerable people have come to rely upon.”

These have included a threat of a £500 parking charge for the vehicle used to transport and distribute food, and demands that the charity obtain a costly waste disposal licence.

Stuart said: “We questioned whether this was proportionate or appropriate for a small, entirely volunteer-run charity carrying out a weekly homeless outreach but, nevertheless, we have now obtained the certificate to ensure we are fully compliant.”

The council has also turned up on several occasions with a group of police and security officers to complain about the soup kitchen, Stuart said. “From our perspective, the scale and manner of these visits have at times felt intimidating and disproportionate given the nature of the work we are carrying out.”

He has asked the council to issue permits to charities for specific days and locations, so they know what is expected of them and can carry out their volunteering without being “blind-sided” by new requirements.

A Westminster city council spokesperson said the soup kitchen was not safe at present.

“Soup kitchens can provide a valuable service but need to be carefully managed. Operators must treat vulnerable people with dignity and take care of the surrounding area,” they said.

“At the moment we have several kitchens operating at the same time and place, leading to large crowds of the most vulnerable people gathering in a confined area.”

The spokesperson said this could lead to drug dealers turning up “looking to exploit the situation”, and that the council had received complaints from residents about “antisocial behaviour, littering and crime in Charing Cross while the soup kitchen is operating”

They added: “Currently, the site is not safe for those using the service or the general public.”

The Conservative council has been taking part in a crackdown on homeless people.

The council’s deputy leader, Caroline Sargent, said of homeless sites in Westminster: “Local people and businesses are fed up with rough sleeping sites springing up, and so are we. This is totally unacceptable in the heart of a capital city.”

articles.title: How a Sudanese refugee became a head teacher in a Chadian camp
articles.excerpt:
Adre, Chad – Sahra remembers growing up in el-Geneina, the capital of Sudan’s West Darfur state, determined to outperform the boys in her class.

After sitting her national examinations in 2005 and 20...
articles.body_text:
Adre, Chad – Sahra remembers growing up in el-Geneina, the capital of Sudan’s West Darfur state, determined to outperform the boys in her class.

After sitting her national examinations in 2005 and 2006, she decided she wanted to become a teacher. She volunteered in classrooms while pursuing a university degree, eventually specialising in education administration.

Then, in April 2023, war between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) tore apart the life she had built.

The conflict has devastated Sudan, forcing millions of people from their homes. Chad, which shares a long border with Sudan to the east, has received a large share of those fleeing the fighting.

Sahra is now among nearly one million Sudanese refugees who have crossed into Chad, helping make it one of Africa’s largest refugee-hosting countries.

In eastern Chad, thousands of families arrived to find little more than open ground and trees to shelter under. For many children, there was no school to return to.

In 2024, Plan International and partner organisations established a primary school in one refugee camp. The school now has 1,059 pupils and 30 teachers – Sahra is the head teacher.

Teachers, administrators and child welfare workers have been recruited from the refugee community, allowing people who fled Sudan to help provide services for families displaced alongside them.

Chad was already facing a serious education crisis before the latest influx of refugees from Sudan. More than two million young people cannot read or write, and, according to the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), three out of four pupils nationwide are taught by people whose own education ended at secondary school.

The refugee influx has added pressure to an education system already short of classrooms, teachers and basic facilities.

“Illiteracy is very dangerous,” Sahra says. “I want the children to be optimistic about the future because education prevents them from early marriage and violence.”

To accommodate the number of pupils, the school runs two shifts, one in the morning and another in the evening. Lessons cover mathematics, science, history, geography, Arabic and French.

But teaching in exile comes with its own difficulties.

Sudanese teachers have had to adjust to Chad’s curriculum while working across language differences. Chadian children may speak local dialects, while many Sudanese pupils speak Arabic.

“The teaching syllabus in Sudan is easy, but the one in Chad is difficult for us,” says Oummalnas, a teacher who fled el-Geneina in 2024. She teaches mathematics and Arabic.

“We need more workshops to improve our teaching skills and adapt to the Chadian system,” she said.

At first, Sudanese and Chadian kids sometimes struggled to get along. Over time, those tensions have eased. The children now learn and play together outside school.

Plan International also provides safe spaces where under-fives can play, socialise and receive psychosocial support in the absence of formal kindergartens.

“We don’t separate education from child protection. It’s an integrated approach that helps create harmony,” said Kefa Mayange, Plan’s Emergency Response Manager for Chad.

For parents in the camp, school is as much about safety as education.

Charfadine arrived with his family during the heavy rains of 2023. Back in West Darfur, his children went to school regularly until the conflict forced them to flee. Three of them now attend primary school in Chad.

“We are happy when they go to school here [in Chad] because it’s a receptive place. It protects them from the violence coming from criminal groups,” he told Al Jazeera.

His hopes remain tied to the country they left behind.

“My ambition is for my children to be teachers to teach coming generations in Sudan and doctors to treat illnesses,” he said.

But not every child has made it into a classroom.

Nasradine, another parent, says hundreds of unaccompanied youngsters who lost their parents while fleeing Darfur remain out of school and wander around the camp.

“If those children remain outside school, our camps will be in danger,” he said. “This group could turn to crime and make our place unsafe. We just want help for those children to go to school.”

For mothers such as Roukhaya and Zenab, memories of their escape from el-Geneina remain vivid. They walked for about 10 hours to reach the Chadian border.

Yet both say life in Sudan, despite the war, had once felt more manageable than life in the camps.

Roukhaya’s children entered formal schooling for the first time after arriving in Chad. But she has watched older teenagers drop out because there are no high schools or vocational training opportunities for them.

Keeping younger kids in school is a daily struggle, too.

Azraa, a Mobile Unit Supervisor with Plan International, and her colleagues go tent to tent, encouraging parents to keep their children in class. In families with six or seven children, parents may send only two or three to school while the others stay behind to collect firewood, fetch water or look for casual work.

Every Friday, community centres hold awareness sessions reminding families that education remains important, even in displacement.

These efforts are happening despite a severe shortage of resources. Kefa says the refugee response in eastern Chad remains one of the most underfunded humanitarian responses in the world.

Children make up more than half of the refugee population, yet the 2026 Sudan Regional Refugee Response Plan received only 17 percent of the funding it required, leaving an 83 percent shortfall. Education remains among the least supported sectors.

At Sahra’s school, the shortage is visible every day.

There are no flush toilets, no electricity and no accessible facilities for children with disabilities. Pupils sit packed together on the ground or share benches.

Teachers and parents are asking for basic improvements: solar panels for lighting, a mobile health clinic, school meals and enough desks for pupils.

Abakar Mahamat Nour, an Education Officer with the Economic and Social Development Agency (ADES), a Chadian nongovernmental organisation supporting education and emergency relief, says the arrival of Sudanese teachers has created an opportunity for solidarity across the border.

“Chad and Sudan are like brothers; we share families,” he told Al Jazeera. “Having people like Sahra coming from Sudan to teach our children is a benefit for our country. They help our students gain new cultural perspectives and build new friendships.”

She lost the life she had built as a teacher and education administrator in West Darfur. In exile, she has found herself doing what she had planned to do all along: teaching children.

“Refugees have skills, experience, and dreams,” said Kefa Mayange, Plan’s Emergency Response Manager for Chad. “Like Sahra, we see them as leaders.”

Note: Full names have been withheld for safety and privacy reasons.

articles.title: Europe's scorched landscapes seen from space after summer heatwaves
articles.excerpt:
The impact of the heat has been noticeable in satellite imagery

The impact of this summer's extreme temperatures on western Europe can now be seen from space after successive heatwaves since May.

Sa...
articles.body_text:
The impact of the heat has been noticeable in satellite imagery

The impact of this summer's extreme temperatures on western Europe can now be seen from space after successive heatwaves since May.

Satellite images examined by BBC Verify show shrunken glaciers, scorched areas left by wildfires, green fields turned arid and lower river levels.

And some landmarks have been affected, too. The Palace of Versailles, south of the French capital Paris, appears as an island of trees surrounded by brown fields in these images.

The EU's climate monitoring service, Copernicus, has confirmed that western Europe experienced its hottest June-to-July period on record.

The immediate cause of the heatwaves has been persistent high-pressure weather systems bringing clear, sunny skies and allowing temperatures to build, according to the Met Office.

But climate change, mainly due to the burning of fossil fuels, has been raising average temperatures for decades and making hot spells much more likely and intense.

We've taken a look at how the sweltering weather has left its mark on landscapes across the continent.

The waters of the Danube, Europe's second-longest river, have dropped to their lowest levels for 30 years in several countries.

This has led to unusual discoveries on the river bed, including the bones of a mammoth in Bulgaria and a sunken WW2 warship in Serbia. You can see the sunken ship has emerged from the deep in the right-hand image below.

And where the river snakes through Hungary and Romania, nuclear power stations have been forced to shut down or run at reduced capacity for some time because of an inability to use river water for cooling.

Meanwhile on the Rhine, some cargo vessels have been left stranded and river cruises have been cancelled.

Even the snow-capped peaks of the Alps have not escaped the heat.

Ongoing measurements suggest this summer could become one of the worst ever recorded for melting Alpine glaciers, with more than a month of the season still to go.

After a mild winter, glaciers had less snow cover than usual at the end of April - and an unusually early heatwave the following month accelerated the melting of snow.

This exposed the ice beneath, leaving the glaciers vulnerable to melting faster in subsequent heatwaves.

As you can see below, satellite imagery suggests much of the front of Rhône Glacier in Switzerland has retreated by 50m (160ft) or more since the same time last year.

In a stable climate, glaciers would be expected to remain more or less the same size over the long-term.

Dr Lander van Tricht, glaciologist at the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology, said in recent years climate change has led to "much less snow in winter and much, much more melt in summer.

"And if we continue this trend, then the future looks very dramatic for the Alps."

Wildfires have transformed parts of western Europe this summer, too.

More than 90,000 hectares (900 sq km or 350 sq miles) has burned in France. This is already its worst year on record, according to the European Forest Fire Information System.

The largest fire in Gironde region, where the city of Bordeaux is situated, burnt about 42,000 hectares of land - roughly equivalent in size to the Isle of Wight.

Part of the reason this year has been particularly bad for wildfires is that land has been tinder-dry.

Dr Douglas Kelley of the UK Centre for Ecology and Hydrology tells us extreme wildfires are becoming "more and more frequent" as climate change is creating ideal conditions, with higher temperatures drying out vegetation and soils faster.

Even zoomed-out satellite imagery of western France shows a striking increase in the browning of land compared to last year.

To assess whether 2026 is unusual we used the Normalised Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), a measure which uses satellite data to assess how green and healthy vegetation is. Lower readings indicate more sparse or stressed vegetation.

The NDVI this summer came in below a five-year benchmark of 2021 to 2025 across about 70% of France. Close to half the UK and roughly 40% of western Germany showed the same.

Prof Andrew Challinor, from the University of Leeds, said the images were "consistent with widespread water stress", which "does not bode well" given much of Europe's land is covered by crops meaning it could hit the agriculture industry and food production.

In the worst-affected areas, soil moisture is lower than on about 98% of comparable dates in the historical record, according to Prof Luis Samaniego, from the Helmholtz Centre for Environmental Research.

And, he warns, even if rain returns, some of the agricultural damage may already have been done.

What do you want BBC Verify to investigate?

Satellite images show impact of heatwaves and drought on UK landscape

'Hotter and hotter and hotter' - Europe's new climate in seven charts

The before and after images showing glaciers vanishing before our eyes

articles.title: BBC was warned of author’s claim to possess missing clothes of child murder victim
articles.excerpt:
Corporation was told of claims by Christopher Berry-Dee that he had clothing, which was lost while in its possession

The BBC was warned by two whistleblowers that a British true crime author was clai...
articles.body_text:
Corporation was told of claims by Christopher Berry-Dee that he had clothing, which was lost while in its possession

The BBC was warned by two whistleblowers that a British true crime author was claiming to have obtained the missing clothes of a child murder victim that the broadcaster had lost.

The Guardian has established that the office of the former head of the BBC and the corporation’s whistleblowing unit were both informed that Christopher Berry-Dee, the UK’s most successful true crime author, had told people he had obtained the clothes of Karen Hadaway, who was murdered in 1986.

Sources have told the Guardian that Berry-Dee was boasting of having had Karen’s clothes during the 1990s and 2000s. In an investigation published today, multiple women have accused Berry-Dee of sexual and violent offences, which he denies.

Karen was killed alongside her best friend, nine-year-old Nicola Fellows, in Brighton’s Wild Park in what came to be known as the Babes in the Woods murders. The clothes she was wearing were obtained in 1991 by the journalist Martin Bashir, who was working on a possible BBC documentary about the case, but were subsequently lost.

The mystery of what happened to Karen’s clothes has dogged the corporation since 2004, when a police detective asked for them to be returned, only for the BBC to realise it could not find them. The corporation later apologised and paid a financial settlement to Karen’s mother.

In the late 1980s Berry-Dee campaigned for police to return Karen’s clothes to the Hadaways. He then sought to persuade the parents to give them to him in turn by offering to arrange for cutting-edge DNA testing. He described the Hadaways handing him the clothes “with tears in their eyes” in his book A Question of Evidence.

The clothes then appear to have been returned before being given to Bashir in August 1991. Eileen Fairweather, a freelance journalist working with Bashir on an investigation into the murders, was present when Karen’s mother handed her daughter’s clothes over. They “were in a bin liner … inside was a clear plastic evidence bag”, she said. “You could see the bloodstains.”

Fairweather, who had tried for years to find out what became of the missing clothes, began reinvestigating in 2021 after a BBC inquiry concluded Bashir had forged evidence to trick Diana, Princess of Wales into giving him an interview in 1995.

Fairweather’s sources told her Berry-Dee had boasted about having the clothes during the 1990s and 2000s. She also discovered he had twice been arrested, and once charged, for alleged child sexual abuse, though never convicted.

The whereabouts of the clothes remains unclear. Berry-Dee told the Guardian it was “100% correct” he had obtained them and claimed to have since burned them, but did not respond when asked to explain the timeline or clarify whether he had obtained them a second time after Michelle Hadaway gave them to the BBC.

A lawyer for Bashir said he had no recollection of Berry-Dee. “[He] left the clothing at the BBC’s Public Eye offices. That is where his actions vis-a-vis the clothing ends,” the lawyer said.

Fairweather contacted the BBC’s whistleblowing unit in 2022 to tell them she believed Berry-Dee was the last person known to be in possession of Karen’s clothes. The corporation said its senior leadership was reviewing the allegations, only to inform her three years later it was closing the case with no further action.

A second warning was emailed to the office of the then BBC director general, Tim Davie, by Ian Heffron, an uncle of Nicola Fellows, after Davie apologised to a parliamentary committee on the corporation’s behalf for having lost the clothes.

“Could you please have urgent enquiries made into the following,” Heffron wrote. “Have the BBC ever employed or been associated with the author Christopher Berry-Dee in any way?” He added: “My reason for asking is because I am given [to] understand that this man has stated that he had possession of Karen’s clothes.”

Heffron received a response from Davie’s office confirming receipt of his email but never heard anything further.

The BBC declined to comment on whether it took any action in response to the emails from Fairweather and Heffron. A spokesperson said: “In 2023 we apologised for falling short in our duty of care to Michelle Hadaway and reached a settlement with her regarding the loss of her daughter Karen’s clothes. We believe this matter has been investigated as thoroughly as possible.”

articles.title: Is the US ready for President Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez?
articles.excerpt:
The New York congresswoman’s power is in the spotlight as people wonder if the stars are finally aligning for her to run for US president in 2028

“They assume that my ambition is positional. They ass...
articles.body_text:
The New York congresswoman’s power is in the spotlight as people wonder if the stars are finally aligning for her to run for US president in 2028

“They assume that my ambition is positional. They assume that my ambition is a title or a seat. And my ambition is way bigger than that. My ambition is to change this country.”

The words were delivered slowly, deliberately and with some steeliness by Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. Her audience, crammed into the pews of Rockefeller Memorial chapel at the University of Chicago, burst into spontaneous applause. That was in May. In the three months since, the speculation around Ocasio-Cortez’s ambitions – for herself and for America – has only grown louder.

Friends and foes alike wonder if the stars are aligning for the New York congresswoman to run for US president in 2028. They point to voters raging against the machine – including the ageing Democratic party establishment – and hungry for change. They note how progressives pushing for economic justice and universal healthcare have won a string of impressive victories in mayoral elections and congressional primaries over the past year.

Then there are the opinion polls. Last month a Granite State Poll from the University of New Hampshire found Ocasio-Cortez leading a potential Democratic field in that crucial state. She has the kind of name recognition that money can’t buy, nearly 10m followers on Instagram alone and fans ranging from the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) to Nancy Pelosi, the former speaker of the House of Representatives.

As Barack Obama, Donald Trump and Joe Biden showed, presidential elections have a habit of finding the right person at the right time in the right place. Ocasio-Cortez, a 36-year-old with a progressive agenda and can’t-be-taught social media smarts, could meet the moment for a nation eager for a fresh start after a decade of Trumpism.

If modern politics is about pendulum swings, it is hard to imagine anyone who better personifies a rebuke of the octogenarian Trump and his nativist “Make America great again” (Maga) movement. This week a Zogby Strategies national poll found that a generic democratic socialist candidate leads generic Maga candidate 45% to 33%.

Ashik Siddique, a co-chair of the DSA, of which Ocasio-Cortez is a member, said: “If she were to throw her hat in the ring, there would be a lot of excitement for it from members of Democratic Socialists of America. We definitely want to see a strong working class voice in the 2028 presidential primary.”

Ocasio-Cortez has not ruled out a run for president and her actions have done nothing to quell the notion of a campaign in stealth mode. Last year she joined her mentor, the independent senator Bernie Sanders, on a “Fighting Oligarchy” tour that drew huge crowds. More recently she has crisscrossed the country to support progressive candidates, further enhancing her national profile.

In the past week alone she made two moves that intensified political pundits’ chatter. First Ocasio-Cortez used Instagram to announce that she is freezing her eggs, a decision she described as a move to “feel more in control of my life”. She acknowledged the “political risk” in sharing personal family planning details but stated her goal is to normalise conversations about the professional and personal challenges women face. The internet quickly became awash in speculation that Ocasio-Cortez ended her relationship with and engagement to long-time partner Riley Roberts , driven by reports from Puck News and others noting she had long since stopped appearing with him in public and mentioning his name.

Then, when asked by ABC interviewer Jonathan Karl about the cultural battles of the 2020 pandemic era – including calls from some on the left to defund the police – she laughed and, quoting a New York city council ally, remarked: “Woke One was crazy” – apparently trying to draw a strategic line between hard-fought struggles for racial justice and the performative excesses of lockdown isolation that became an easy target for the right.

Unlike many would-be presidents of the time, Ocasio-Cortez does not appear to be driven by personal ego, according to those who knew her, which may prove to be her political superpower. She was a volunteer organiser for Sanders’ 2016 campaign, his first presidential run and one that built a national movement around his vision of democratic socialism, even as he lost to former secretary of state Hillary Clinton.

When she decided to run for office herself, the former bartender and waitress had virtually no money but was assisted by progressive organisations such as Brand New Congress and Justice Democrats. In 2018 she beat 10-term incumbent congressman Joe Crowley, a member of the Democratic leadership and potential future speaker, in a New York primary.

Corbin Trent, her first communications director in the House of Representatives and the co-founder of Justice Democrats, was there on the night she ousted Crowley. He recalls that the political industrial complex began trying to map her career path before the ink on the ballots was even dry.

“Primary night, she beats Joe Crowley,” he recalled. “I get phone calls from elected officials and other people and their question is, what’s next? What’s the pathway here? What’s she going to run for? What higher office would she seek? This is literally a few hours after the polls close in the primary. That’s the way DC thinks. Not, hey, what can we do with Medicare for all or this or that or any of the other things?”

As Ocasio-Cortez’s national profile exploded – bringing in $15m in her first electoral cycle and attracting unprecedented demands from foreign heads of state – Trent tried to lay out a long-term strategic map. He suggested upstate New York events to prepare for a statewide Senate run. But she resisted the logic of political careerism.

“To my chagrin and frustration that never was a way in which she could plan or operate. She did not have an idea in her head of this ultimate prize of president or governor or senator.”

Instead, Trent argues, her appeal lies in a rare authenticity – an ability to validate the deep-seated economic anxiety of Americans. “Alexandria has two things going for her. She’s genuinely curious about other people. It’s not like she has to pretend to be. I’ve had politicians ask me, ‘How can I be more genuine?’ Well, that’s probably not going to help if you have to fucking ask me that.

“Two, she is genuinely open about herself. Some people believe that nobody cares what they think or who they are and then other people don’t want you to know who they are. She doesn’t suffer from either of those failings.”

Other observers agree that Ocasio-Cortez has that X factor missing from so many professional politicians: relatability. Chris Scott, a political strategist who served as the coalition director for Kamala Harris’s 2024 presidential campaign, said: “When you talk about AOC’s humble beginnings being a bartender that’s a lived experience story that resonates, especially with millennials, with their upbringing.

“What you are starting to see – whether it’s conservative or progressive - is people are leaning more and more towards candidates with lived experience that they feel they relate to as politics gets more polarising.”

That said, Ocasio-Cortez has now been in Washington long enough to draw accusations of going from outsider to insider. The activist who critiqued the establishment and championed the Green New Deal has spent recent years working closely with Democratic leadership. This week she received warm praise from Pelosi, who told a Politico summit in Sacramento, California: “I think that she has been so operational, and it’s just wonderful. I know it’s a joy to work with her.”

The transition has caused some on the far left to wonder if the system has simply co-opted its most dangerous critic. Cenk Uygur, a controversial political commentator and co-founder of the online progressive news show The Young Turks, watches Ocasio-Cortez’s recent evolution with a mixture of policy agreement and tactical despair.

Ocasio-Cortez has described Israel’s actions in Gaza as a “genocide” and last month voted to block US military aid to the country. But Uygur has not forgotten her high-profile appearance at the 2024 Democratic National Convention, where she delivered a rousing speech praising vice-president Harris’s efforts to secure a ceasefire in Gaza — a claim that many leftwing activists viewed as a dishonest whitewashing of the administration’s complicity in the conflict.

“Why did she basically fib on Kamala Harris’s behalf during the DNC and pretend that Kamala Harris cared about Palestinians and was trying to keep the Israelis in check?” he said. “Because she secretly loves Israel? No, it’s because she wanted to prove to mommy and daddy that she’s a good girl. If you’re a good girl you support Kamala Harris and, if you need to, you fudge her record.

“Then you go tell Jonathan Karl that your side is ‘crazy’ and you changed and you can’t explain what you changed into or how you changed or why you changed. But the message is super clear both for the establishment and progressives: ‘I’m not going to challenge the system so establishment, you can rest easy, I’m not a threat.’ And they have rested easy. That’s why she’s getting enormously positive coverage.”

The 2028 Democratic presidential primary election is expected to be crowded and noisy. If Ocasio-Cortez runs, she might face challenges from fellow progressive Congressman Ro Khanna of California along with heavyweights including Harris, Pete Buttigieg, Gavin Newsom and Jon Ossoff. Some Democrats, scarred by Clinton and Harris’s defeats in 2016 and 2024, might be reluctant to nominate Ocasio-Cortez out of perceived expediency if they believe the US is still not ready to elect its first female president, a fear expressed by former first lady Michelle Obama among others.

The congresswoman faces another potentially formidable hurdle. Centrist Democrats have long argued that the democratic socialist wing of the party might succeed with white, college-educated voters but struggles to connect with African American communities, pointing to primary races where progressive insurgents have hit a wall. That could prove decisive in an early primary state such as South Carolina.

Nina Turner, a national co-chair of Sanders’ 2020 campaign, who has just been travelling in South Carolina, said: “There are some rumblings in some segments of the Black community that DSA and progressives in general are not doing what it takes to court Black voters and in some ways are leaving us behind for other people who are of colour but not Black.

“That’s real and so DSA as well as progressives are going to have to do something to say, no, we understand the Black plight and we understand that the survival of working-class people comes through Black liberation. They have not done a good job of doing that. I’m hoping that they will.”

Antjuan Seawright, a Democratic strategist in South Carolina, suggests that Ocasio-Cortez’s national viability depends on her remaining a disciplined team player who addresses universal, kitchen-table concerns. He said: “I would love her to run as far away as she can from being any sort of liability in places where we know we have to win in November where we’ve lost before because people have been used as a weapon of mass political destruction and distraction.

“If she continues to talk about health care in such a way that is accessible and affordable for all Americans without burning down the system, but making some alterations to the system, she will be a positive voice to the conversation.”

If she runs, Ocasio-Cortez can also expect a crude onslaught from Republicans and a rightwing media machine that has spent years demonising her as a radical communist who threatens the essence of America. Her “Woke One was crazy,” comment has been seen as an attempt to assuage the concern.

Tara Setmayer, a former Republican communications director on Capitol Hill, said: “That was a very interesting strategic decision to do that and that’s her way of trying to moderate. But she’s palling around with Bernie Sanders and hasn’t completely, as far as I’m aware, repudiated [the influencer] Hasan Piker and some of those leftwing folks. People are not going to forget that and, in this day and age of the internet, it lives forever.”

Setmayer, cofounder of the Seneca Project, a women-led, bipartisan political super political action committee, argues that, instead of campaigning for the White House, Ocasio-Cortez could seek to cement her legislative power by challenging Chuck Schumer for his New York Senate seat.

“If I were advising her, given the failures, unfortunately, of women candidates for the Democrats over the last two election cycles, it would behoove her to run for Senate,” Setmayer said. “She’s almost guaranteed to win that Senate seat.

“It would provide her more gravitas and she’s young enough that she could do a term or two – or a term and a half like Barack Obama – and then run for president. I don’t think that she can go from being a congresswoman to a serious presidential candidate without some time in the Senate.”

History, however, is littered with examples of White House aspirants who waited their turn and missed their moment. There are others, such as Obama, who said “carpe diem” and rode a wave all the way into the Oval Office.

Ocasio-Cortez, who would beat Theodore Roosevelt and John F Kennedy to become the youngest US president in history, has said her ambition is way bigger than that. The calling to change America may prove irresistible.

Kurt Bardella, a political commentator and former congressional aide, said: “When you look at the current trajectory of the Democratic party, she is the natural successor to the Bernie Sanders-Elizabeth Warren coalition. She is one of the most gifted communicators in all of politics.

“She is someone who engenders a tremendous amount of passion, either for or against. She does possess the unique quality of: people give a shit. She’s got a lot more going for her than most people. She never has to worry about standing out. The attention vacuum that we live in, and the way that content works, she is in a league of her own.”

articles.title: Concerns grow over increased global ties with Taliban in Afghanistan
articles.excerpt:
Campaigners fear deeper diplomatic contacts are undermining demands for improvements in human rights

The Taliban in Afghanistan have launched a diplomatic effort to end their isolation as major regio...
articles.body_text:
Campaigners fear deeper diplomatic contacts are undermining demands for improvements in human rights

The Taliban in Afghanistan have launched a diplomatic effort to end their isolation as major regional and international powers show a readiness to engage more closely with the repressive regime despite its systematic human rights abuses.

Five years after the Taliban took power, an increasing number of countries are renewing ties or scaling up diplomatic contacts with the hardline Islamists, who seized power in Kabul in 2021 after 20 years of brutal insurgent warfare.

Campaigners fear that the individual contacts by different countries risk undermining “coherent, consistent” demands for an improvement in human rights in return for any diplomatic concessions.

The United Nations described a recent “cascade of [Taliban] edicts and laws” that have banned women from universities and most employment, denied teenage girls education and imposed strict dress codes. Minorities have been persecuted, while activists and journalists face repression. Afghanistan has become a “graveyard for human rights,” the UN said in March.

India, Qatar, China, Iran and several central Asian states all recently welcomed Taliban officials or opened new channels of communication. Russia, which recognised the Taliban government in Kabul just over a year ago, signed a military cooperation agreement last month. In June, the European Union held talks with Taliban officials in Brussels about returning failed asylum-seekers to Afghanistan. Individual European countries have also deepened their own contacts with Kabul.

“There is no doubt there has been an evolution. The Islamic emirate is now in a confident position. They have realised they are indispensable for regional countries right now and even with Europe and the US they have identified how to engage,” said Shivam Shekhawat, at the Observer Research Foundation in Delhi.

“The Taliban see any kind of contact as a diplomatic win and they have been able to capitalise on that as a sign granting legitimacy to the regime.”

A strict policy of isolation imposed after the Taliban seized power in 2021 towards informal or “de facto” recognition is now fragmenting. Some western commentators have suggested more countries recognise the regime. Others want intensified “back channel” engagement.

“We are not against any engagement … There is a need for engagement even if just for aid agencies to mitigate the ongoing humanitarian crisis but we are worried about the end goal of these contacts and the discussions that are taking place,” said Fereshta Abbasi, Afghanistan researcher at Human Rights Watch.

“There should be a consistent and coherent message from the international community to the Taliban that they will not have any friends if they do not show real progress in terms of the women’s rights and human rights situation … and that is not happening.”

The new contacts stem from a combination of regional security concerns, pressure in the west to reduce illegal immigration and a general recognition that the Taliban are unlikely to be forced from power in the foreseeable future.

The European Commission downplayed its discussions in Brussels with a Taliban delegation, the first such formal encounter since 2021, as merely “technical” and focused on returns, but a Taliban spokesperson claimed it was a historic visit that was a step towards regularising consular relations with EU countries.

“You cannot condemn Taliban abuses in one breath and then announce talks on immigration in the next … The Taliban are telling their constituency back home that they are now accepted by the international community,” said Abbasi.

This year officials from Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan have all visited Kabul or other Afghan cities, seeking trade routes and pipeline deals that would allow their landlocked countries access to seaports or third countries beyond.

India too has moved to reinforce relationships that were frosty after the fall of Kabul to the Taliban in 2021, in part to exploit new tensions between the movement and the Islamist movement’s historic sponsors, Pakistan.

New Delhi secured a sanctions waiver last year so that Amir Khan Muttaqi, the Taliban foreign minister and a veteran official who has spent decades at the heart of the movement, could travel there.

In June, India’s UN envoy suggested a rethink was necessary on sanctions, such as travel bans, asset freezes and arms embargoes, that target dozens of Taliban members.

“The political reality of Afghanistan has changed in the last five years, and the current UN sanctions regime must take that into account,” said Harish Parvathaneni.

Afghan authorities’ diplomatic strategy has involved hosting envoys in Kabul, including those from China, Japan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia. Last year, Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, made the first visit by an Iranian foreign minister to Kabul for almost a decade.

The Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan “seeks relations with all countries”, Taliban spokesman Zabihullah Mujahid said, though “the countries of the region and our neighbouring states have particular importance, because our economic ties and interests are closely linked”.

Anna Borshchevskaya, a senior fellow at The Washington Institute focusing on Russia’s policy towards the Middle East, said Moscow had multiple reasons for recognising the Taliban regime and seeking closer relations.

“One likely objective is simply having allies … Afghanistan is also very significant for Russia geographically and Russia just wants influence in that part of the world. There was an opening and they were able to take it,” Borshchevskaya said.

“It’s a very cold, cynical calculation. It’s part of a very simple zero-sum view that for Russia to win the US has to lose. From the Kremlin perspective, this is a global battle and whether you are looking at Europe or Afghanistan or wherever, it’s one geopolitical chessboard.”

Britain has said it pursues a policy of “limited and pragmatic” engagement with Taliban officials, largely through the UK Mission to Afghanistan based at the British embassy in Qatar. Discreet meetings with the Taliban have also repeatedly been held by other western countries in Qatar. In Germany and at least four other western European capitals, key consulates are now controlled by the Taliban, not representatives of the former Afghan government.

Taliban officials have also sought cross-border infrastructure projects to boost the country’s fragile economy and diplomacy. Natural resources are another lure for overseas powers. Kabul has expanded the mining sector, attracting firms from neighbouring China and elsewhere.

China, which is worried about Islamic militancy on and around its south-western borders, has welcomed Taliban officials in recent years, and hosted talks when Afghanistan and Pakistan went to war earlier this year.

The Taliban are split, with deep disagreements on the ban on women’s education among other issues, but remain dominated by the most conservative factions. Recent laws have further reinforced repression, designating many religious minorities, including Shia Muslims, as heretics and imposing strict punishments to silence dissent.

Other new laws recognise only “excessive” beating as domestic violence against women and facilitate the marriage of girls without their consent.

Analysts do not believe the Taliban are likely to moderate their position in the near future and point to the continuing authority of Hibatullah Akhundzada, the reclusive and authoritarian cleric leader.

Ramin Mansoori, a researcher at the University of Pittsburgh and Carnegie Endowment who studies Afghan politics, said the Taliban’s priority was its domestic agenda.

“They are not going to make any significant concessions. Most of them don’t have an international perspective,” Mansoori said.

articles.title: ‘My heart breaks into a million pieces’: emotional tributes to Kumanjayi Little Baby at Alice Springs funeral
articles.excerpt:
Hundreds gathered with flashes of pink to farewell the five-year-old girl, who was allegedly murdered in April

Warning: This story contains references to Indigenous Australians who have died

Get our...
articles.body_text:
Hundreds gathered with flashes of pink to farewell the five-year-old girl, who was allegedly murdered in April

Warning: This story contains references to Indigenous Australians who have died

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A sombre funeral service for Kumanjayi Little Baby has been attended by hundreds of people from the Alice Springs community and surrounds.

Wearing pink and some dressed in T-shirts bearing the face of the five-year-old girl, the crowd gathered under grey skies in the red centre capital on Saturday.

Family members surrounded a small coffin adorned with flowers and cried together.

The girl’s grandfather, Robin Japanangka Granites, opened the funeral to the public to allow the community to grieve as one.

“You come because you are one of our family,” he told them.

“You are from here and we need you because we both cried at that same time.”

In a eulogy read on her behalf, Kumanjayi Little Baby’s mother, Jacinta Roy, urged that her daughter be remembered for who she was.

She was a girl who loved watching shows like Masha and the Bear and Bluey, as well as playing games on her mum’s phone, Roy said.

The young girl also loved cuddling puppies and the colour pink.

“As a mother, my heart breaks into a million pieces,” she said. “I miss her.

“As a Christian, I would like to thank Father, Son and Holy Spirit for gifting me with a beautiful, precious little baby girl for the precious time that I was her mother here on Earth.”

The family of the allegedly murdered girl invited the desert community to farewell her on Saturday while embracing her favourite colour, pink.

The service comes months after her disappearance sparked one of the largest searches in Northern Territory history.

Kumanjayi Little Baby – as she is known for cultural reasons after her death – went missing on the outskirts of Alice Springs in late April.

It prompted an intensive five-day search by emergency services and local volunteers in grassy bushland.

The discovery of her body prompted a nationwide outpouring of grief, with vigils held across the country.

A 47-year-old man is awaiting trial after being charged with her murder.

Japanangka Granites, a Warlpiri elder, thanked locals for their efforts to locate Kumanjayi Little Baby and for their support of his family.

Kumanjayi Little Baby would be with our “father in heaven”, he said at the time.

Indigenous Australians can call 13YARN on 13 92 76 for information and crisis support; or call Lifeline on 13 11 14 or Mensline on 1300 789 978

articles.title: Taiwan passes defence budget after record delay, retains drone funding
articles.excerpt:
Taiwan’s opposition-controlled parliament has approved the government’s annual budget, preserving funding for a drone programme central to the island’s defence plans against China.

Lawmakers passed t...
articles.body_text:
Taiwan’s opposition-controlled parliament has approved the government’s annual budget, preserving funding for a drone programme central to the island’s defence plans against China.

Lawmakers passed the $93bn budget late on Friday, after a record 266 days of political deadlock and its legal deadline, as President William Lai Ching-te’s administration, which lost its parliamentary majority in 2024, continues to clash with opposition parties over government spending.

The approved funding was earmarked for drone development, despite an earlier threat by the main opposition party, the Kuomintang, to slash that funding by 70 percent.

The Kuomintang dropped the proposed cut after concluding there was no wasteful overlap between the development and procurement programmes it had initially cited as justification.

Other reductions included a 60 percent cut to special allowances for government agency heads, a 2.5 percent cut to military equipment and facilities spending, and a 50 percent cut to media policy and publicity budgets.

Before Friday’s vote, the government had been operating under a provisional budget mechanism to keep paying civil servants and funding welfare programmes.

Legislative Speaker Han Kuo-yu, following the vote, said the prolonged delay had caused “social division and a constitutional impasse”.

He called on both the ruling and opposition camps to seek greater compromise going forward.

Lai said in a statement that parliamentary oversight and review of the budget are an important constitutional duty.

In May, the same opposition-controlled legislature cut a proposed $40bn special defence budget by 38 percent, stripping out all funding for domestically produced combat drones and leaving only United States arms purchases intact.

Taiwan’s military currently holds fewer than 5,000 drones, while China is reported to have ordered close to a million for delivery this year, part of a broader regional buildup that includes Ukraine’s target of seven million drones in 2026.

Beijing claims self-ruled Taiwan as its own territory and has sharply escalated military pressure on the island in recent years.

articles.title: Wisconsin Democratic candidate says her party 'left behind' rural America
articles.excerpt:
Blue Dog Democrat Rebecca Cooke spoke about how the party needs to rebuild its relationship with rural and working-class voters that the party had "left behind" in recent years.

Blue Dog Democrat Reb...
articles.body_text:
Blue Dog Democrat Rebecca Cooke spoke about how the party needs to rebuild its relationship with rural and working-class voters that the party had "left behind" in recent years.

Blue Dog Democrat Rebecca Cooke, a Wisconsin congressional candidate, discussed in an interview Thursday how she is trying to set things right after she accused her party of abandoning rural and working-class voters in recent years.

She appeared on the "Politics War Room" podcast with co-hosts James Carville and Al Hunt, known for calling out the far left of the Democratic Party.

"I don’t wanna put you in a box, but you say you’re a Blue Dog and a New Democrat, tell me what it means to be a Blue Dog Democrat," Hunt asked.

"They are folks that are fiscally conservative, socially liberal, are really working from, like, a place-based perspective," Cooke said. "They're people that understand rural Democrats, working-class Democrats, that are showing up in rural communities and working-class spaces that historically our party has left behind. And that's like I think why I was connected with them originally or why I — you know what they were doing resonated with me so much."

JAMES CARVILLE PREDICTS 2028 DEMOCRATIC PRIMARY WILL TEST TRUE STRENGTH OF PARTY'S SOCIALIST WING

Rebecca Cooke talked about her working-class origins and her work as a waitress, suggesting that doing such jobs gives people like her more of a connection with Americans' real kitchen table issues than many other politicians. (Kayla Wolf/Getty Images)

She cited multiple examples of other moderate Democrats who "understand how to talk to people in rural America where I feel like a lot of folks in the Democratic Party don't anymore, and I certainly do."

"I think we've built strong coalitions across this district with farmers, you know, healthcare workers, people in rural communities that feel really left behind," Cooke added.

Hunt cited her past comments, "You've said that in Congress, Republicans are too right-wing and congressional Democrats are too left-wing. Specifically, how has Hakeem Jeffries [been] too left-wing?"

"I'm talking just, I think, in general when I talk — I did an ad last cycle where I was standing in the middle of the road on my parents' farm talking about how folks in DC are either too far left or too far right, and we need more people in the middle that want to work across the aisle to get things done," she said. "I'm somebody that wants to work in a really bipartisan way and not put, you know, party before people or politics before people, and I think that's I think what's important."

Cooke suggested that the Democratic Party needs more candidates from a working-class background, citing her own experience.

"I've been a waitress since I was 16 years old," she said. "I've run a small business here in my community but I also waitress to make ends meet. I did some fellowships last year also, with the group called Third Way, around, you know, how do we get more working-class folks to run for office? How do we connect more with working-class voters in general?"

"And I'm proud of that work because I think there's this disconnect in the party and when we run working-class people, folks come out to vote because people trust those people, right? Folks trust me because I have some of the same lived experience that they they've had, right?," Cooke added.

HAKEEM JEFFRIES DOUBLES DOWN ON 'MAXIMUM WARFARE' RHETORIC, TELLS CRITICS 'I DON'T GIVE A DAMN'

Cooke's campaign noted a recent statement from her that if she sees somebody in a MAGA hat, she’s going to shake their hand and introduce herself . (Brett Carlsen/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

She cited other examples from her life, saying many politicians cannot relate to such experiences.

"We've had to sell our cows because of the low price of milk," Cooke said. "I've had to struggle to compete with the Amazons of the world in running a small business. I know what it's like to sign the front of a paycheck as well as the back of a paycheck, right? And I know what it's like to do hourly wage work. There's a lot of members of Congress that have never done those sorts of things. So when they're making policy that's impacting working families, they're out of touch with that."

Fox News Digital reached out to Cooke's campaign, asking what specific issues she would push for the Democratic Party to moderate on to win back rural and working-class voters.

"Rebecca grew up on a dairy farm and has been campaigning in every county, rural and urban, in the 3rd district because she wants to earn support from Wisconsinites of all backgrounds, including Republicans and Trump supporters," a spokesperson said. "

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Rebecca Cooke grew up on a farm and suggested that experiences like that have made her more politically aware of everyday kitchen table issues than most other politicians. (iStock)

"On MSNOW this week, she said if she sees someone with a MAGA hat, she’s going to shake their hand and introduce herself," the spokesperson continued. "She’s running to fight for working people and has no problem disagreeing with other Democrats, like when she said she’d ‘stand up to Democrats to fight for a secure border,’ she ‘support[s] funding the police fully, and doesn’t believe in universal student loan forgiveness because it only sticks a bandaid on a structural problem.’"

Alexander Hall is an associate editor for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to Alexander.hall@fox.com.

articles.title: California teen faces prison after viral video shows him squaring up, repeatedly kicking sea lion in the face
articles.excerpt:
Tyler Muehl, 18, was captured on video attacking the mammal in San Diego. (KTTV)

A California teenager pleaded guilty Friday to repeatedly kicking a sea lion in the face and chasing the animal as it ...
articles.body_text:
Tyler Muehl, 18, was captured on video attacking the mammal in San Diego. (KTTV)

A California teenager pleaded guilty Friday to repeatedly kicking a sea lion in the face and chasing the animal as it tried to escape, according to video of the attack.

Tyler Muehl, 18, who lives in the San Diego seaside neighborhood of La Jolla, entered his plea in a federal courtroom to a misdemeanor violation of the Marine Mammal Protection Act’s prohibition on harassing wildlife, the Justice Department said.

"Federal crime. Federal consequences," U.S. Attorney Adam Gordon wrote in a statement.

SUSPECT IN VIRAL MONK SEAL HARASSMENT VIDEO SAYS HE WAS DOXXED AS FEDERAL COURT FIGHT BEGINS

Tyler Muehl, 18, repeatedly kicked a sea lion in the face before chasing the animal in San Diego, the Justice Department said. (KTTV)

The incident was investigated by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). Muehl admitted to kicking the sea lion on July 22, as the mammal was peacefully sitting on a seawall, federal prosecutors said.

"Intentionally striking or kicking a marine mammal is not only illegal — it is dangerous for the well-being of the animal," said NOAA official Eric Morgan.

The teen approached the animal with his hands squared up, as if he were preparing to fight, authorities said. As he made his approach, Muehl referred to himself as Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) fighter Max Holloway.

He then kicked the animal four times, "which caused the sea lion to rear, flinch, and immediately recoil," prosecutors said.

EL-SAYED IN THE HOT SEAT AFTER 'SICKENING' ANIMAL CONTROL RECORD GOES VIRAL ON SOCIAL MEDIA

Tyler Muehl, 18, seen attacking a sea lion in San Diego on July 22. He pleaded guilty on Friday to violating the Marine Mammal Protection Act’s prohibition on harassment of wildlife. (KTTV)

"After the second kick, the sea lion turned and tried to flee, but Muehl chased after the animal and kicked at it a third time," a DOJ news release states. "As the sea lion tried to get away, it stumbled on the sea wall as it fled."

Officials said the teen kicked the sea lion again and chased it until the animal made its escape.

As part of his plea agreement, Muehl said the video, which went viral online, was a "fair and accurate recording of what occurred."

People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (PETA) commented on the incident on its social media accounts.

"Assault is ASSAULT, no matter the species," the group wrote on X in a July 24 post. "Leave animals ALONE, and always speak up when you witness abuse."

Tyler Muehl seen in video footage attacking a sea lion on July 22 in San Diego. (KTTV)

Muehl faces up to one year in prison and $100,000 in fines. He is expected to be sentenced on Oct. 20.

Fox News Digital has reached out to Muehl's attorney for comment.

Louis Casiano is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to louis.casiano@fox.com.

articles.title: Delta flight diverted twice after lavatory leak floods cabin, leaves passengers stranded for hours
articles.excerpt:
A routine maintenance test flight over northwest England drew widespread attention after its flight path appeared to spell out "I'm bored" on the Flightradar24 flight-tracking website.

A Delta Air Li...
articles.body_text:
A routine maintenance test flight over northwest England drew widespread attention after its flight path appeared to spell out "I'm bored" on the Flightradar24 flight-tracking website.

A Delta Air Lines flight traveling from Paris to Seattle was forced to make an unexpected stop in London after the crew reported a mechanical issue involving an onboard lavatory, the airline said.

Delta Flight 81 departed Paris-Charles de Gaulle Airport on Aug. 13 bound for Seattle-Tacoma International Airport when the issue prompted the flight crew to divert to London Heathrow Airport.

The Airbus A330-900 was carrying 209 passengers and 13 crew members at the time, according to information provided by Delta.

As the aircraft approached Heathrow, the flight crew declared an emergency with air traffic control because the plane would be making an overweight landing, the airline said.

FLAMES SHOOT FROM AMERICAN AIRLINES FLIGHT BEFORE EMERGENCY LANDING

A Delta Air Lines aircraft taxis at London Heathrow Airport in London on Oct. 7, 2016. Delta Flight 81 diverted to Heathrow after its crew reported a mechanical issue involving an onboard lavatory. (Simon Dawson/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Despite the emergency declaration, the aircraft landed normally and safely at Heathrow.

Delta maintenance personnel then serviced the Airbus in London in an effort to address the lavatory-related mechanical issue.

"We apologize to our customers for their experience and delay on Delta Flight 81 from Paris-Charles de Gaulle to Seattle, which diverted to London Heathrow after the crew reported a mechanical issue involving an onboard lavatory," a Delta spokesperson said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

"This is not the experience we strive to provide, and we're focused on getting our customers to their destinations as quickly and safely as possible."

LIVE BULLET FOUND ABOARD UNITED FLIGHT FORCES PASSENGERS OFF PLANE FOR SECURITY SWEEP AT DENVER AIRPORT

A Delta Air Lines Airbus A330-900, registration N812NW, is pictured at Leonardo da Vinci–Fiumicino Airport in Italy on July 8, 2025. Delta Flight 81 was operated by an Airbus A330-900 carrying 209 passengers and 13 crew members when it diverted to London. (Massimo Insabato/Archivio Massimo Insabato/Mondadori Portfolio via Getty Images)

Once maintenance work was completed, the aircraft was able to depart Heathrow — but the disruption meant passengers still faced an additional detour before reaching their intended destination on the West Coast.

Instead of continuing directly from London to Seattle, the flight headed to New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport because of the crew's available duty time, according to Delta.

Passengers cleared U.S. Customs at JFK before continuing their journey to Seattle.

The unusual itinerary ultimately took the 209 passengers from Paris to London, then across the Atlantic to New York before they could continue on to Seattle.

Passengers prepare to board a flight at London Heathrow Airport on June 27, 2026. Delta Flight 81 made an unscheduled stop at Heathrow while traveling from Paris to Seattle after its crew reported a mechanical issue. (Marc Fernandes/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Delta did not provide additional details about the specific mechanical problem involving the lavatory or what maintenance was required to address it.

Brittany Miller is a Fox News Digital breaking news writer and former Independent reporter who graduated from Syracuse University in 2023.

articles.title: Reagan National Airport makes drastic change following deadly 2025 midair collision
articles.excerpt:
FOX Business correspondent Grady Trimble has the latest on the new radar system on 'America Reports.'

A new radar system has been installed at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in the Washing...
articles.body_text:
FOX Business correspondent Grady Trimble has the latest on the new radar system on 'America Reports.'

A new radar system has been installed at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in the Washington, D.C., area following a 2025 midair collision that killed 67 people due to multiple systemic failures.

The airport has received the Surface Movement Radar, known as SMR-4, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Friday. The technology will help air traffic controllers identify aircraft and vehicles moving along runways and taxiways, even in bad weather and low-visibility conditions.

"This new radar is our latest reinforcement tool to equip our controllers as they safeguard our air travel. We’re working at the Speed of Trump to deliver the world-class air traffic control system America deserves," Duffy said.

AIR TRAFFIC CONTROL AUDIO CAPTURES TENSE MOMENT TWO PLANES NEARLY COLLIDED AT BOSTON LOGAN AIRPORT

A new Surface Movement Radar Model 4 (SMR-4) has been installed at the Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport (DCA), which came more than a year after a deadly midair collision that killed 67 people. (Department of Transportation)

He said the new radar system will give air traffic controllers a "clearer portrait" of airport activity.

Reagan Airport is the fifth airport to receive the system. Newark Liberty International Airport received the technology earlier this week.

Over the next three years, $30.5 million will be invested in safety and technology upgrades at Reagan National, the Transportation Department said.

The new upgrades came after the Jan. 29, 2025, midair collision between American Airlines Flight 5342, a regional jet operated by PSA Airlines, and a U.S. Army Black Hawk helicopter over the Potomac River near the airport.

FAA INVESTIGATES SOUTHWEST NEAR MISS AFTER AIR TRAFFIC CONTROL SENDS JETS ON COLLISION COURSE

Rescuers on a boat work next to the wreckage of a Black Hawk helicopter at the site of the crash after it collided with the American Eagle flight 5342 which was approaching Reagan Washington National Airport and crashed into the Potomac River, outside Washington, U.S., January 30, 2025. (Kevin Lamarque/Reuters)

All 64 people on the American Eagle flight and three aboard the military helicopter were killed.

The federal government admitted liability for the deadly collision. The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said systemic failures in airspace design, safety oversight, and risk management by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and the Army contributed to what happened.

"This complex and comprehensive one-year investigation identified serious and long-standing safety gaps in the airspace over our nation’s capital," said Jennifer Homendy, chairwoman of the NTSB, in a January 2026 report. "Sadly, the conditions for this tragedy were in place long before the night of Jan. 29."

Louis Casiano is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to louis.casiano@fox.com.

articles.title: Lebanon’s PM urges timetable for Israeli withdrawal as Hezbollah slams deal
articles.excerpt: Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam is pushing for a clear timetable for Israel’s withdrawal from Lebanese territory, as Hezbollah’s leader accuses Lebanon’s government of exposing the country’s own a...
articles.body_text:
Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam is pushing for a clear timetable for Israel’s withdrawal from Lebanese territory, as Hezbollah’s leader accuses Lebanon’s government of exposing the country’s own army to disgrace by pursuing the deal at all.

According to a statement released by the prime minister’s office on Friday, Salam met United States ambassador to Beirut Michel Issa and General Joseph Clearfield, who heads the US military coordination group for Lebanon, to discuss the military track of the negotiation framework with Israel, along with the latest developments in southern Lebanon.

“Salam stressed the need for Israel to stop destruction operations, expand the scope of pilot areas, and set a clear timetable for Israeli withdrawal from Lebanese territory,” the statement said.

Lebanon’s Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri met the same US officials separately.

“Israel has not stopped its violations and attacks on Lebanon,” he said, citing continued village demolitions, bulldozed farmland, forest fires and damage to heritage sites.

“The key to stability remains forcing Israel to stop its war and withdraw to the international border.”

Issa called the talks “positive” and said negotiations would continue, without giving a date for the next round.

Hezbollah chief Naim Qassem hit back on Beirut’s remarks, accusing Lebanese officials of putting the army under “undue pressure” by implementing a non-functional agreement.

“How can you accept this ongoing humiliation of the Lebanese army, exposing it to bombardment and Israeli pressures, instead of acting as its protectors?” Qassem said on Friday.

He accused Israel of trying to bind Lebanon to an oversight body controlling the army’s deployment and internal operations.

Qassem pointed out that Israel has kept striking homes and demolishing tunnels inside Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh, the first designated pilot zone, despite the Lebanese army’s presence there.

He challenged officials to “name a single achievement from the seven rounds of negotiations”.

US Ambassador Issa, meanwhile, told reporters Israeli attacks would stop only once Hezbollah disarms.

“If they give up their weapons, everything will stop,” he said.

The June trilateral framework, to which the US is also a party, involves the disarmament of Hezbollah and a gradual withdrawal of Israeli forces from Lebanon’s south, where it has occupied several areas. The gap between the two sides remains wide.

Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said on Thursday that Israel will not withdraw until Hezbollah is disarmed, as Israeli forces currently occupy multiple towns inside the Lebanese border.

The Israeli military has continued to occupy Lebanon’s southern area, demolishing homes and displacing residents across the territory.

The next round of talks is expected to resume in early September.

Lebanese authorities say Israel’s attacks since March 2 have killed 4,335 people, wounded 12,277 and displaced more than a million.
