The location was not public but he traveled to New York City and emailed UnitedHealthcare leadership, posing as an institutional investor, to get more information, getting a response within an hour.

He also researched who would be attending. Mangione then said he printed a gun with a 3-D printer and affixed it with a silencer. “I shot Mr Thompson in Manhattan and he died,” he continued. “When I did so, I understood that my actions would place him in fear of death or serious bodily injury. I knew what I was doing was illegal.”

Judge Margaret Garnett accepted the plea and will sentence Mangione on 18 December. Mangione’s lawyer also confirmed to the judge that there is no plea agreement with the government. He will remain in federal custody as he awaits sentencing. He faces life in prison.

Mangione, 28, entered the plea at a hastily scheduled hearing in Manhattan federal court this morning, resolving one of two cases against him in connection with Thompson’s killing. With this guilty plea, his lawyers could seek to have the state case – for which he has pleaded not guilty to murder and is scheduled to go on trial next month – thrown out on double jeopardy grounds.

Mangione has stood. He’s being escorted out of the courtroom by Marshals.

Judge Garnett sets Mangione’s sentencing for 18 December.

Judge Garnett now asks: “Mr Mangione how do you now plea to counts 1 and 2 in the indictment?”

Garnett, saying she found him competent and able to enter a plea, goes on: “I will accept your guilty plea and enter a judgment of guilty on counts one and two in the indictment.”

Mangione’s allocution is done and the prosecution is now going over what evidence it would have presented at trial; they’re now saying some of the evidence includes video of the shooting.

Mangione said that he endured physical pain for years.

“I shot Mr Thompson in Manhattan and he died,” he continued.

“When I did so, I understood that my actions would place him in fear of death or serious bodily injury,” he said. “I knew what I was doing was illegal.”

The judge reveals there is no plea deal. Instead, the government has filed a letter saying what they believe an appropriate sentence should be.

Garnett said: “The government indicates that it believes the applicable sentencing range … 292 to 365 months of imprisonment.”

articles.title: National Rail acknowledges ‘exceptional challenges’ of extreme heat after second train derailment in 24 hours
articles.excerpt:
Incident near Essex town of Wickford happens day after two passengers seriously hurt in East Sussex derailment

The UK’s fifth heatwave of the summer has “presented exceptional challenges to the railw...
articles.body_text:
Incident near Essex town of Wickford happens day after two passengers seriously hurt in East Sussex derailment

The UK’s fifth heatwave of the summer has “presented exceptional challenges to the railway”, Network Rail has said, after two trains derailed in less than 24 hours.

On Friday, British Transport Police confirmed the rear carriages of a Greater Anglia train derailed “in an upright position” at Wickford railway station in Essex, adding that there were no reported injuries. On Thursday, two people were seriously injured when several Southern train carriages left the track near Lewes in East Sussex and ended up on their side, trapping passengers onboard.

Martin Frobisher, the group safety and engineering director at Network Rail, said it was “working quickly to understand the situation and to provide assistance where needed”.

He urged people to avoid speculating on the cause of the derailments Wickford and in Lewes and said that Network Rail would conduct internal investigations to look at causes and factors.

The derailed train in Essex was travelling from Southend to Liverpool Street with about 40 people onboard. It left Rayleigh at 2.06pm but failed to reach Wickford at 2.11pm as planned.

A post on the National Rail website said all lines were closed between Wickford and Southend Victoria. This meant trains running between London Liverpool Street and Southend Victoria were unable to operate.

The Rail Accident Investigation Branch (RAIB) said on X that it had deployed a inspectors to the site to gather evidence.

A major incident was declared by BTP on Thursday afternoon after the incident near Lewes. About 150 people had been on the service from London Victoria to Eastbourne, which was evacuated. Two people were taken to major trauma centres with severe injuries. BTP said on Friday the injuries were not deemed to be life-threatening.

Southern urged customers planning to travel this weekend to check ahead as significant disruption was expected across parts of the network until further notice. Trains are expected to be extremely busy, with customers advised to allow at least one extra hour for their journey.

Frobisher said: “The unprecedented hot and dry weather that we have experienced this summer has presented exceptional challenges to the railway. In response, we have taken several additional proactive steps to manage and mitigate the impact on the railway, including closely monitoring the temperature of tracks, implementing speed restrictions where it is appropriate to do so, and planning track renewals around high temperatures.

He added: “We will also conduct our own internal investigations, in which we will look at all possible causes and factors. I appreciate the public will be concerned at the news of two derailments of passenger trains over a short period of time, but I want to reassure them that Britain’s railways still rank among the safest in the world and that safety is always our first consideration on the railway.”

John Whitehurst, the chief executive of Greater Thameslink Railway (GTR), which operates Southern, praised four railway workers onboard the train – the driver, onboard supervisor, a spare driver and an off-duty member of staff – who initial reports suggested had “acted quickly to help make the railway safe and support passengers during the evacuation”.

“Their actions are a powerful example of colleagues putting passengers first in very difficult circumstances,” he said.

After the incident, Whitehurst insisted the railway was safe in hot weather. He told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme that derailments were “incredibly rare”, adding that what happened “was a very serious incident and I’m deeply saddened by it”. He said “a full investigation” was under way with the RAIB.

Richard Bowker, a former chair of the Strategic Rail Authority, told the same programme that the inquiry would look at the effects of heat on the damaged track, including whether the ground below the track had dried out.

James MacCleary, the Liberal Democrat MP for Lewes, told Times Radio that concerns had been raised about tracks being “a bit bumpier in recent months” in the area as a result of the sustained heatwaves.

Gareth Dennis, a railway engineer and author of How the Railways Will Fix the Future, said although there was no firm evidence to connect the two derailments, “the likelihood of two similar derailments in the hottest part of the country happening in quick succession without a common cause is extremely low”.

He added that there was a high likelihood that the derailments were caused by a track buckle, where steel rails that have expanded in the heat snap into a buckled shape under the wheels of a passing train, though there are other possible causes.

Xueyu Geng, a professor in ground engineering at the University of Warwick, said steel rail was known to expand significantly in extreme heat, with a 1C (1.8F) rise in temperature causing approximately 11mm of expansion per kilometre of track.

A Department for Transport spokesperson said: “We are aware of a derailment involving a Greater Anglia train near Wickford, Essex. The train is upright, there are no reported injuries and investigators have already been deployed to the site.

“Our railways remain amongst the safest in the world and while incidents like this are extremely rare, when they do occur, they are taken very seriously.”

articles.title: ‘It’s due to climate’: the people of Stourbridge on the town’s wildfires
articles.excerpt:
Thursday has been described by residents as ‘horrendous’, ‘distressing’ and ‘one of the scariest days of my life’

People in Stourbridge have described the fires that devastated more than a dozen home...
articles.body_text:
Thursday has been described by residents as ‘horrendous’, ‘distressing’ and ‘one of the scariest days of my life’

People in Stourbridge have described the fires that devastated more than a dozen homes as “horrendous” and “distressing”, with one describing blazes that surpassed the height of residential houses.

Multiple fires spread across the West Midlands on Thursday as temperatures reached record highs of 38.1C in the UK, during the country’s fifth consecutive heatwave.

Fifty-four people, including 19 who were taken to hospital, were treated at eight different fires yesterday, West Midlands ambulance service said, with the fire service confirming 19 homes in Stourbridge, a market town in Dudley, had been fully destroyed and an additional 18 damaged.

During a visit to Stourbridge on Friday, Andy Burnham said the UK was like a “tinderbox” and announced the commission of firefighting planes to tackle future wildfires. “I’ve never seen scenes like this anywhere in Britain,” he told the BBC.

The Guardian spoke to people who were forced to hurriedly evacuate from their homes in Stourbridge on Thursday, as a wildfire spread near the town’s golf course. They repeatedly praised the support and efforts of local authorities and neighbours, but are yet to return home, with some staying at a nearby hotel or a makeshift evacuation centre that had been set up at a local boarding school.

Gemma Hobbs, 46, and her partner, Andy, 61, were evacuated from their home on Osmaston Road on Thursday, as the wildfires raged over a mile away. Andy described seeing a house in flames.

Gemma said: “I looked out the windows and all I could see was thick black smoke. My husband came home in a bit of a flap and said: ‘We’ve got to get out. We’ve got to get out immediately.’”

Andy added: “It’s just the fact you don’t expect something to be as exponential as this so quickly. From the span of the area, it’s over 40 acres, that’s what we’ve been told.”

Gareth Jones, 59, was providing shelter to his neighbour John Bairner, who had to be evacuated overnight and said it was a “scene of devastation”, calling the wildfire “terrifying”. “It was probably one of the scariest days of my life yesterday,” he said. “It was just the speed at which it spread, it was devastating. Absolutely frightening how quickly it spread. Within an hour. It’s a major event.”

Bairner added: “All of the fields have gone, they’re all black. There’s a lot of residents up there, with buckets, hoses, just dampening down because it’s still smouldering away up there.”

The Old Swinford hospital, a boarding school in Stourbridge, was set up as a makeshift evacuation centre for affected people late on Thursday. As queues of cars and volunteers dropped off donations and supplies on Friday, the headteacher of the school, Paul Kilbride, described the fires as a “devastating experience”, with more than 20 people evacuated from a nearby care home.

“From what I saw, [the evacuees] were very tired and very anxious. I think they also showed great spirits [and] they obviously want to go home now,” he said. “This community suffered a lot yesterday”.

Laurence Green, 66, stayed at the Old Swinford hospital boarding school overnight after he was evacuated from his home on Osmaston Road. Green said he saw “plumes of smoke” yesterday afternoon before he was directed by police to evacuate to the town hall.

“It’s horrendous … Some of the houses look as though they are very badly damaged or completely destroyed,” he said. “People who built up their lives and built up their homes and for some people, it’s all gone.”

Green agreed the devastation was a wake-up call for local people and the country about the impact of climate change. “We should have woken up to what’s happening climate wise,” he said, before calling on the government to make the issue a priority. He dismissed the temporary ban on disposable barbecues, announced by Burnham on Friday, as “pathetic” in comparison.

“I had a bit of an argument with one of the Conservative councillors about it because I said: ‘It’s due to climate’ and he told me: ‘We shouldn’t be bringing politics into it’. Well, yes we should.”

The Bishop of Dudley, Martin Gorick, was also evacuated from his home and echoed Green’s concerns. He said climate change had to be taken seriously and the country had to become less reliant on fossil fuels. “The heat yesterday was extreme,” he said. “That doesn’t happen in England normally.”

“This is not a divisive issue. It’s something that should bring us all together because we all live in one world. This is our only world.”

Gorick described witnessing houses “ablaze” and described it as a “pretty awful sight”. “You see bursts of flame when it hits a tree or something like that. The flame is above the height of houses, it’s big and hot,” he said.

The bishop, however, praised the local community for rallying together in the face of the devastation, including individuals who put together a list of medications needed by those who had been evacuated, and local churches and mosques who provided bedding.

“The shops responded. People giving away drinks and food,” Gorick said. “It was great to see Muslims and Christians coming together, as well as any volunteers from any background, Sikh, Hindu, no faith were coming together.

“That’s the best side of the Black Country, coming together in a crisis.”

articles.title: People detained at Mississippi ICE facility sickened by gas leak and denied medical care
articles.excerpt:
Facility also had no air conditioning for two days amid extreme heat, according to one of the people detained

People detained at an overcrowded federal immigration camp in Mississippi were sickened b...
articles.body_text:
Facility also had no air conditioning for two days amid extreme heat, according to one of the people detained

People detained at an overcrowded federal immigration camp in Mississippi were sickened by a mystery gas leak, then denied medical care when they complained of headaches and other symptoms, it has been alleged.

A lengthy power outage at Adams county detention center, an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facility run by the private operator CoreCivic, also left it without air conditioning for two days this week, according to one detainee who contacted the Guardian through his family.

As a result, he said, people detained there were forced to spend hours outside in near 100F heat in blazing sunshine and with no shade, or left to swelter inside in cramped cells.

Tensions at the center, he said, were rising, and more arguments and physical altercations were taking place between people there, leaving him and others fearful of violence that he said inadequate staffing levels would not be able to handle.

The allegations come as a third person who was held in ICE custody at the Delaney Hall detention center in New Jersey, run by the GEO Group, another government contractor, was reported to have died; and an inspection report of the Adams county facility in Natchez found 23 violations of use-of-force or restraint standards.

Those deficiencies, found by inspectors from ICE’s office of detention oversight in May, led to the downgrade of the Adams county’s facility rating from superior in 2025 to acceptable/adequate this year.

The gas leak is said to have occurred last Saturday.

“They evacuated them out into the afternoon heat for hours,” said the wife of the detainee, whom the Guardian is not identifying by name for fear of retaliation.

“They were outside for hours. And when they came back in, it still smelled of gas. And then some of the men were getting headaches and symptoms of inhaled gas. They were never really told where the leak came from, how it was resolved, or was it fully resolved.

“Illness has been growing. So there are a lot of people getting sick, and they have begun putting people three to a cell that was designed for two.”

The power outage, the detained person reported, happened on Monday. Electricity was partially restored on Tuesday, he said, allowing lighting and other essential operations to function, but air conditioning remained out until late Wednesday.

“When these things are happening, either they’re shut out outside without shade and air conditioning, and they’re not given any answers,” the detainee’s wife, a US citizen, said. “Or a lot of the time the power was out they just had them locked in their cells, they didn’t get to leave for dinner or breakfast.

“There’s generators that run the defenses and things to make sure no one can escape, but they were without air conditioning for two days, and in Mississippi it’s very hot right now.”

The wife of the person detained said her husband told her authorities were clamping down on efforts by those incarcerated to “spread word” about the conditions.

“They didn’t give them the tablet devices during that time because they didn’t want them notifying loved ones,” she said. “If they feel anyone’s organizing anything they’ll send them to solitary.”

The Adams county facility is one of the nation’s largest immigration jails, and the only dedicated one in the state, although CoreCivic also conducts detention operations for ICE inside the private Tallahatchie county correctional facility in Tutwiler.

Mississippi Today reported in March that the 14-acre Natchez jail holds more than 2,000 detainees, but that only 9% of those detained had any kind of criminal record. The person who contacted the Guardian has an active asylum application for a green card. He has no criminal record, and was arrested by ICE in January at a routine appointment.

CoreCivic, which has headquarters in Tennessee, operates dozens of detention and correctional facilities around the country, many under contract to ICE. The company reported a 26% rise in revenue to $2.2bn in 2025, which Patrick Swindle, its president and chief executive officer, credited to “the trust of our government partners”.

At the same time, CoreCivic has come under increasing scrutiny for conditions and treatment of detainees inside its vast network. In April, Human Rights First published a damning report into alleged “widespread due process violations, inhumane conditions, and lasting physical and psychological harm inflicted on families” at the South Texas family residential center, an ICE detention camp for families in Dilley.

Last month, a court-appointed monitor found major flaws in care provided to detainees at the California City detention center near Los Angeles, including significant gaps in emergency care, failures to provide medications in a timely manner, inadequate screenings for health conditions and a lack of accommodations for people with disabilities.

A 2021 homeland security department inspection of the Adams county facility found “violations of ICE detention standards that threatened the health, safety, and rights of detainees”, including one episode in which a sick detained person was not sent to the hospital for urgent medical treatment and subsequently died.

Ryan Gustin, CoreCivic’s senior director of public affairs, said in a lengthy statement that the Guardian had “received some bad information” about the gas leak and power outage.

“While several detainees thought they may have smelled something related to a natural gas leak, none of our staff members detected anything along these lines,” he said. “Out of an abundance of caution, an on-call facility maintenance staff member came in to assess the facility for any possible gas leaks, and none were found.

“There was a storm on Monday that caused a power outage which impacted the facility and the surrounding community for approximately two hours. ACCC is equipped with emergency generators, and they operated as designed during the outage.

“When the power was restored, a transformer went out and had to be replaced by the local power company. This caused the lights in the common area of one housing pod to stay out. At no point were there any interruptions to the facility heating, ventilation or air conditioning (HVAC) systems.”

Gustin said at no time was anybody refused medical treatment. “We are committed to providing safe, humane and respectful care for everyone entrusted to us,” his statement said in part.

“Our clinic is staffed with licensed healthcare professionals including physicians, nurse practitioners, psychiatrists, psychologists, mental health counselors and dentists who contractually meet the highest standards of care, as verified by multiple audits and inspections.”

The Workers Circle, a New York-based Jewish social justice organization that assists families and loved ones of people who are detained, said it was alarmed by the allegations.

“No human being should be forced to endure the dangerous and inhumane conditions that have been reported here,” said Jessica Burroughs, the group’s national organizer for freedom vigils that it has conducted at ICE facilities nationwide for more than a year.

“We will continue to call attention to these reports until they are thoroughly investigated and addressed with the urgency they warrant. And we will demand accountability from those responsible to bring an end to these abuses once and for all.”

articles.title: French court blocks Macron’s social media ban for under-15s
articles.excerpt:
Constitutional council says curbs infringe freedom of expression and privacy as president vows to rework legislation

France’s top court has blocked a ban on social media access for under-15s, ruling ...
articles.body_text:
Constitutional council says curbs infringe freedom of expression and privacy as president vows to rework legislation

France’s top court has blocked a ban on social media access for under-15s, ruling that it infringed freedom of expression and privacy.

The decision is a blow to President Emmanuel Macron as momentum builds around the world for Australian-style restrictions on children’s use of social media.

A law approved by parliament in July would have barred under-15s from opening social media accounts from the beginning of September. Tech platforms would also have been required to close existing accounts within four months and use age-verification tools approved by ⁠France’s privacy regulator.

However, the constitutional council found that while the law required users to provide proof ​of age, it failed to specify the “conditions and limits” ‌under which this should happen. It also found that the restrictions infringed freedom of expression and privacy.

“The council holds that the contested provisions, on ‌the one hand, disproportionately infringe upon the freedom of expression and communication and, on the other, fail to provide the legal safeguards necessary to ensure the right to respect for private life,” it said.

Several countries have followed the example of Australia, which barred under-16s from leading social media platforms in December last year. Indonesia and Malaysia have introduced restrictions for under-16s on certain platforms, while the UK is preparing to block leading apps for the same age group next year.

In Australia, the affected platforms are Facebook, Instagram, Kick, Reddit, Snapchat, Threads, TikTok, Twitch, X and YouTube.

The EU has also said it plans to seek stronger protections for children from harmful social media features, building on the digital services act that already sets rules for tech platforms.

Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, said last month that “it is clear we need age-appropriate restrictions to platforms”. She did not refer to a specific age limit, instead raising the prospect of “phased and gradual access for different age ranges”.

Social media companies generally oppose blanket bans, arguing that they already have measures to protect younger users, including a minimum age of 13. They ⁠have also said they would comply with government restrictions.

Macron, who in April ​urged teenagers to turn off their devices and read in order to become better ​citizens, has asked the French prime ‌minister, Sébastien Lecornu, to ​rework the legislation to address the constitutional council’s concerns, according to the Élysée.

The Élysée said Macron remained determined for the reform to take effect before spring 2027, when France holds its presidential election. Macron is ineligible to stand for a third term.

articles.title: Elephants may have played surprising role in early human survival, study suggests
articles.excerpt: A tourist was moved to tears when his lifelong dream of seeing wild elephants finally came true in Thailand. Guided by a tour leader, he and his partner encountered a roaming elephant family just ahea...
articles.body_text:
A tourist was moved to tears when his lifelong dream of seeing wild elephants finally came true in Thailand. Guided by a tour leader, he and his partner encountered a roaming elephant family just ahead—an emotional moment that left him overwhelmed.

Elephants are widely adored by many people today — but a recent study suggests early humans were butchering them for survival nearly 2 million years ago.

A group of international researchers found what they describe as "the earliest direct evidence of proboscidean butchery," including a newly identified elephant butchery site, according to an article published in the spring in the journal eLife.

Modern elephants are the only living proboscideans today — a group that once included woolly mammoths and mastodons. The animal bones belonged to Elephas recki, an extinct elephant species.

ANCIENT HUMANS WERE HUNTING AND EATING SHARKS 7,000 YEARS AGO, BURIAL SITE DISCOVERY SHOWS

The research centers on Olduvai Gorge, a site in northern Tanzania's Serengeti Plains known for major discoveries of early human fossils and tools.

At the site, excavators found stone tools alongside bones of ancient elephants — and the recent paper, written by archaeologists and paleoanthropologists, suggests the remains were likely deliberately butchered by early human ancestors.

The remains of ancient elephants that were found in Tanzania (not pictured) point to systematic processing by early human ancestors. (Universal Images Group via Getty Images)

The bones date back some 1.8 million years, during the early Pleistocene epoch.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Though researchers have observed evidence of humans hunting large megafauna in later periods, the discovery suggests that early humans processed elephant carcasses more systematically.

"The food surplus generated by the exploitation of some of these animals would have been a significant advantage."

The study also says that early humans' ability to butcher large animals "represents a unique evolutionary trajectory, with no direct modern analogue."

The discovery centers on Olduvai Gorge, pictured above — a site long known for major early human fossil and tool findings. (iStock)

"This shift in behavior is accompanied by larger, more complex occupation sites, signaling a profound ecological and technological transformation," the paper states.

"Rather than opportunistic scavenging, these findings suggest a strategic adaptation to megafaunal resources, with implications for early human subsistence and social organization."

Meat from large animals like elephants would have provided a significant food source for early humans, the paper notes.

Elephant meat may have provided a substantial food surplus for early human groups, researchers say. (iStock)

"The food surplus generated by the exploitation of some of these animals would have been a significant advantage for the survival and adaptation of the hominin groups," the study adds.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Fox News Digital reached out to the study's lead researcher for comment.

Researchers continue to uncover new clues about human diets, spanning from ancient civilizations to the earliest humans.

The discovery points to elephants playing a key role in early human diets and survival strategies. (Marica van der Meer/Universal Images Group)

This past December, archaeologists in Pompeii uncovered preserved food remains revealing what enslaved people ate before Mount Vesuvius erupted.

More recently, researchers identified food DNA on the Shroud of Turin, suggesting that Jesus' alleged burial shroud may have been contaminated over time.

Andrea Margolis is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital and Fox Business. Readers can follow her on X at @andreamargs or send story tips to andrea.margolis@fox.com.

articles.title: Trump administration argues that ballroom construction is ‘vital’ for national security in appeal to supreme court – US politics live
articles.excerpt:
Administration that halting construction will leave Trump ‘much less safe’ after appeals court ruled work lacked necessary approval from Congress

Trump administration asks ⁠US supreme court to allow ...
articles.body_text:
Administration that halting construction will leave Trump ‘much less safe’ after appeals court ruled work lacked necessary approval from Congress

Trump administration asks ⁠US supreme court to allow construction of White House ballroom

The Trump administration, in its appeal to the supreme court today, said that “this case involves an extraordinary and unlawful injunction that will halt the ongoing construction of the integrated military complex including a totally secure ballroom space, at the East Wing of the White House, which is vitally required by national security.”

It’s worth noting that the appeals court ruling blocks the above-ground construction of the ballroom, but would allow the work on the underground security structure to continue.

However, the government argues that “every part” of the project is “an integrated whole geared toward remedying security deficiencies and bringing critical improvements to the White House”.

The administration add in the filing: “The entire ballroom structure is designed to shield the military installation beneath it.”

Hands Off the Arts, an artist and worker advocacy coalition, have released a statement in response to the Kennedy Center’s vote to once again to move forward with Donald Trump’s controversial plan to temporarily shutter the building for substantial renovations, which includes inscribing Trump’s name on the facade.

“The Kennedy Center belongs to the American people – not one man,” the statement reads. “This vote is fatally flawed for a simple reason: To our knowledge, the board vote proceeded without figures showing how much money the institution currently has or any analysis of how a closure of this scale would affect its operation. The Center consistently has refused to release the full financial picture of profit and loss to the board or the public.”

“This paves the way for more corruption,” it continues. “The President is using the Kennedy Center as another lure for people to influence him openly. The more projects that he can ‘create’ that need private donations—Freedom250, the Ballroom, FIFA events—the more avenues he has to accept gifts from people who have government interests.”

The Kennedy Center board – mostly handpicked, staunch allies of the president – voted “to close the Kennedy Center’s main building” for renovations despite a federal order for Trump’s name to be removed from the signage.

In May, the US district judge Christopher Cooper ordered Trump’s name to be removed from the building’s facade after the president had it added last year. Cooper ruled that the addition had been illegal, as only Congress had the authority to change the institution’s name. The center removed Trump’s name in June, but is appealing the decision.

Donald Trump has confirmed that Kevin Rideout, an American missionary who was kidnapped in Niger in October, has been released back to the US.

“I am proud to announce that Kevin Rideout, a wonderful Christian Missionary, is back in United States Custody,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform on Friday. “Kevin, the United States of America looks forward to welcoming you HOME. Glad to have helped!”

Rideout, a 50-year-old missionary pilot, was kidnapped in the west African country’s capital, Niamey, on 21 October by three armed individuals and was probably driven out of town, according to a security official at the time. No armed group claimed responsibility for the abduction.

Serving in Mission International, Rideout’s organization, said earlier that he “is in good health in the care of US officials” and would soon be reunited with his extended family. Rideout had been working in Niger for 19 years as a missionary before the incident.

The woman accused of vandalizing the World War II memorial in Washington DC appears to have live streamed the incident on Facebook.

A Facebook account under the name of the suspect, Melissa L Farris, currently hosts an over 30-minute video apparently live streamed on Thursday. The video shows a woman with a can of spray paint who proceeds to spray the memorial.

“It was me, I’m doing it, I did it, it’s on camera,” the woman can be heard saying in the video around the 9-minute mark.

This week, Donald Trump admitted that he took a military jet to leave Turkey after the Nato summit in July, despite leading the press and public to believe he was on Air Force One.

Reports also emerged that the deception included smuggling the president, and some of his closest aides, on to a catering truck to avoid suspicion. In this week’s episode of Politics Weekly America, Jonathan Freedland talks with Tara Setmayer of the Seneca Project about why the White House felt the need to come up with such an elaborate lie to protect Trump.

It’s worth noting that Miller’s Pac has donated to several Republicans in competitive House races this midterm cycle. Politico was first to report on the filings.

These representatives include Tom Barrett, who is fighting to hold on to Michigan’s seventh congressional district. Meanwhile, Bryan Fitzpatrick, Ryan Mackenzie and Rob Bresnehan all received thousands from the Dependable Conservative Leadership Pac as they defend their central Pennsylvania House seats. The latter two congressman flipped their districts red in 2024.

Mike Lawler, the Republican congressman who represents a purple district in upstate New York, said that he does not plan to return the $10,000 his campaign received from the Max Miller’s Dependable Conservative Leadership Pac. Miller is facing several domestic abuse allegations from his ex-wife, and has faced calls from both parties to end his re-election bid and resign from Congress.

In an interview on Thursday on CNN, Lawler defended his decision to keep the funds, when pushed by anchor Dana Bash.

“I know Max very well. I’ve talked to him personally over the last two years about this very difficult family situation. It’s tragic. I don’t think anybody disagrees about that. But this is something that should play out in family court,” Lawler said. “Max has been accused. Max has also made accusations against his ex-wife. It is tragic, and obviously I don’t condone any level of abuse. But ultimately, there has been nothing that has been corroborated here.”

According to Lawler’s most recent campaign finance reports he has more than $4.8m cash on hand. When asked why he wouldn’t return the Pac funding, given that it makes up a fraction of his available funds, Lawler said “the allegations have not been verified”.

He added: “If there’s evidence that Max did something, then obviously there should be a thorough investigation of that, but thus far there’s been nothing to verify any of the claims that have been leveled.”

Donald Trump also decried the vandalism on the World War II memorial in Washington DC. “THERE CAN BE NO GREATER INSULT TO THOSE AMERICAN HEROES ,” Trump wrote in an all-caps missive on Truth Social.

However, the president repeated his claim that another monument, the reflecting pool, was subject to vandalism. This, despite the justice department dropping the charges against David Hearn, the former Olympian accused of ripping part of the pool’s lining off. Jeanine Pirro’s office said in a court filing that the actual cause of the damage was a “botched” renovation as opposed to vandalism.

A woman was arrested on Friday morning in connection with the vandalization of the second world war memorial on the National Mall in Washington DC, the capital’s federal prosecutor announced.

Jeanine Pirro, the US attorney for the District of Columbia, announced mid-morning that a suspect was in custody and had been charged with federal crimes.

The memorial had graffiti scrawled on it and the pool polluted with soapy bubbles.

Pirro added that the justice department is filing two felony charges against the suspect, who is now in custody. “Offenses that carry penalties of up to ten years in prison,” Pirro posted on X, showing two images of a middle-aged woman, one of her with what appears to be a can of spray-paint at the scene.

“Vandalizing our World War II Memorial is a despicable attack on a sacred monument honoring the Americans who fought and died for our freedom. Those Americans include my father and grandfather,” Pirro added in the post.

US Park Police had been investigating who graffitied the words “Clean hands dirty $” in red paint on the memorial on Washington DC’s National Mall for the second world war and vandalized the fountain with soapy bubbles.

The US interior department said: “The public should know we will find the person responsible for this disgusting act” and the non-profit Friends of the National World War II Memorial said the site should not be used for political expression.

The government’s lawyer added that given the recent attempts on Donald Trump’s life – which include a shooting at the White House correspondents’ dinner in April – stalling the “vital construction” of the ballroom will leave Trump “much less safe” and ultimately risk “future presidents’ safety”.

The Trump administration, in its appeal to the supreme court today, said that “this case involves an extraordinary and unlawful injunction that will halt the ongoing construction of the integrated military complex including a totally secure ballroom space, at the East Wing of the White House, which is vitally required by national security.”

It’s worth noting that the appeals court ruling blocks the above-ground construction of the ballroom, but would allow the work on the underground security structure to continue.

However, the government argues that “every part” of the project is “an integrated whole geared toward remedying security deficiencies and bringing critical improvements to the White House”.

The administration add in the filing: “The entire ballroom structure is designed to shield the military installation beneath it.”

The Trump administration has asked ⁠the ⁠US supreme court to allow construction of his controversial $400m ⁠White House ballroom to proceed after ​an ‌appeals ‌court ordered work to halt.

In a case testing Donald Trump’s presidential authority, the Washington-based US ⁠court of ​appeals for the District of Columbia circuit ruled last week that the controversial ‌project lacked the necessary approval from US Congress.

In a filing, Trump’s administration ‌asked the supreme court justices to keep the ​decision by the US court of appeals for ⁠the District of Columbia ​circuit ​on hold ​while it ​prepares ‌a full ​appeal.

The government has appealed a number of lower court decisions to the supreme court this week, in the wake of temporary injunctions over the president’s attempts to curb mail-in voting.

The USS George Washington is en route to the Middle East to relieve the USS Abraham Lincoln, according to reports. This comes after accounts about mental health crises onboard the Lincoln, including attempts from service members to jump overboard and chronic food shortages.

The vessel has been on a record-breaking deployment for more than 200 days, after it was redirected to assist with the military operation in Iran.

Democrats have been demanding answers from the Pentagon in recent days to glean the extent of the issues on board and what is being done to address them. Defense secretary Pete Hegseth said on Thursday that the reports are “completely misrepresented”.

In response, Democratic lawmakers have pushed back. Senator Ruben Gallego of Arizona said that he is in communication with the wife of a service member who has forwarded her husband’s text messages about the conditions on board. “Stop lying and fix the problem,” Gallego wrote on social media, in response to Hegseth’s recent comments.

Senator Mark Kelly, a Democrat and navy veteran, told MS NOW on Thursday that he spoke with a woman who is concerned about her grandson, who works as an electrician on board the USS Abraham Lincoln. “He’s lost 20 to 25 pounds and is struggling with depression. And so-called leaders like Pete Hegseth aren’t doing a thing about it,” Kelly said, while repeating calls for an investigation.

Trump will be in Washington for closed-press meetings until he heads to New York, to deliver his remarks in Garden City at 3pm ET. We’ll bring you the latest as that gets under way.

The United States wants Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to publicly condemn a siege imposed by Jewish settlers in a Palestinian village, US and Israeli officials said on Friday, as settlers pressured residents ⁠by pitching a new tent before ⁠Israeli soldiers arrived and it was ​taken down.

Settlers have been besieging homes in Qusra in the occupied West Bank for almost a week, trapping Palestinians in an area where rights groups say settlers are mounting a concerted effort to seize more land, further eating into territory where Palestinians aim ⁠to establish a state.

The siege has drawn public US criticism: the US Ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee – a strong supporter of Jewish settlement in the West Bank – on Thursday condemned settlers besieging a Palestinian home as “Israeli terrorists”.

A US official and an Israeli official said on Friday White House officials are ⁠pressing Netanyahu to publicly condemn the siege.

This week’s Politics Weekly America looks at Trump’s plane ruse. The President departed on a secret military flight from Turkey to Britain last month, prompted by an Iranian assassination threat. Almost everyone believed he was on Air Force One, turns out he wasn’t.

You can hear all about the elaborate scheme to protect the President here.

Conservative backlash was supposed to put an end to the diversity, inclusion and equity (DEI) movement as companies were warned “go woke, go broke”.

In January 2025, Donald Trump delivered a death knell, ending DEI within the federal government with executive orders and threatening to target companies that still supported it. Companies including Google, Goldman Sachs, McDonald’s and Walmart that had embraced DEI years earlier fell into line and announced an end to their policies.

But new research published Friday and shared exclusively with the Guardian found that companies that resisted the pressure and kept their DEI practices, including Costco, Apple and Delta Air Lines, performed just as well as their competitors who pulled back.

American special operations forces are ready to step up warfighting-readiness exercises with counterparts in the Philippines and other countries in Asia to further strengthen a security alliance and help deter a major conflict in the region, a US military official said Thursday.

Admiral Frank Bradley, commander of the US Special Operations Command, is in the Philippines after a trip to South Korea. He will then head to Japan for talks with military officials.

He is the latest American military top brass to visit key Asian allies in recent weeks to reassure them of Washington’s commitment to the region given the US preoccupation with the war in Iran .

Bradley’s command, which has about 80,000 personnel and is based at MacDill Air Force Base in Tampa, Florida, undertakes the US military’s most sensitive and dangerous covert operations. The majority of his forces are deployed in more than 80 countries worldwide, Bradley said.

Russia believes the United States is deeply involved in Ukrainian ⁠attacks against it and has raised the issue with Washington, Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said in comments broadcast on Friday.

He said ⁠that the alleged ⁠US support ​included the supply of intelligence.

“We have submitted a series of questions to the State Department requesting comment, including on the ⁠matter of intelligence data and the fact that the U.S. is far more deeply involved in organizing and executing strikes deep within Russian territory ⁠against civilian targets. We await a response,” Lavrov told state TV.

No immediate comment was ​available from the US.

Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.

President Donald Trump plans to highlight his record on crime and safety during a visit to New York on Friday, pivoting to one of his strongest issues as he looks to boost Republicans in battleground races ahead of the November midterms.

Trump is visiting the Nassau County Police Academy in suburban Long Island, where the White House said he will release new FBI crime statistics showing a decrease in violent crime for 2025.

“President Trump promised to make America safe again and the data proves he has done just that,” White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said. “Unlike Defund-the-Police Democrats, President Trump will always stand with our law enforcement officers and deliver safer American neighborhoods.”

Trump’s visit is aimed at boosting Republican candidates in closely contested races across his home state, but just how much his presence will help is in question as he faces lagging approval ratings and a deeply unpopular war in Iran with no end in sight.

Trump narrowly won Nassau County in 2024, flipping it for Republicans for the first time in more than two decades. It’s home to two Democratic House seats that Republicans now see as winnable this fall, and it’s home turf for Nassau County executive Bruce Blakeman, the Trump-endorsed Republican challenging Democratic Governor Kathy Hochul.

Luigi Mangione, the man accused of gunning down a ⁠health insurance executive, is due in federal court on Friday for a hearing where he is expected to plead guilty to stalking or similar charges. There is more on the story here.

The battle over the Kennedy Center’s future escalated Thursday as President Donald Trump’s allies on the board took new steps to commemorate him with physical changes to the iconic performing arts institution that could defy a federal court order.

The Pacific-based aircraft carrier USS George Washington began heading toward the Middle East, according to reports. This comes as Democratic lawmakers have demanded answers of about mental health crises and supply issues aboard the long-deployed USS Abraham Lincoln.

White ⁠House deputy ⁠national ⁠security adviser Andy ​Baker is ⁠leaving the Trump ⁠administration ​in ‌the coming ‌weeks, Axios ‌reported on Friday. The White House ‌did not respond ​to a request ⁠for comment outside ​business hours. ​The report has not been independently ​verified.

articles.title: Activists try to deliver aid to Palestinians in homes besieged by Israeli settlers
articles.excerpt:
Access to the homes has been blocked by settlers since Sunday

Activists have tried to delivered supplies to Palestinians whose homes in the occupied West Bank have been besieged for days by Israeli s...
articles.body_text:
Access to the homes has been blocked by settlers since Sunday

Activists have tried to delivered supplies to Palestinians whose homes in the occupied West Bank have been besieged for days by Israeli settlers.

The group left water and food near one of the houses in Qusra where two Palestinian families have been trapped since Sunday, with their power and water supplies cut off.

Two of the residents said Israeli forces had prevented the activists from delivering the aid directly to them, and the supplies had to be left outside. The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) denied this.

Also on Friday, a number of settlers returned to set up a tent near the site - a day after an operation to disperse them from the area. It was later removed by Israeli forces.

The IDF said Qusra was a "closed military zone" and so Israeli civilians - who were among the activists - could not enter the area.

"But they weren't prevented from transferring aid to the Palestinian homes in Qusra."

It said in a further statement that Israeli civilians had erected a tent in the Qusra area earlier on Friday, "and IDF soldiers operated to remove it while protecting the local residents".

About a dozen Palestinian households were told to leave their properties during the operation to disperse settlers on Thursday, including members of the Abu Ridi and Hassan families living in two of their three besieged homes.

Qusra Mayor Abdul Azim Wadi told the BBC that Israeli forces were using some of the vacated Palestinian houses as barracks.

The Israeli military said the aim was "to protect the residents" and soldiers had been "instructed that the Qusra residents will remain in their homes".

A spokesperson had previously described the settlers' actions as "deplorable" and "unacceptable", adding that the government would investigate and arrest those responsible.

Watch: How Israeli settlers are besieging Palestinian family homes in West Bank

The situation in Qusra began on Sunday when settlers blocked the road to the Palestinian families' gates and cut off their power and water supplies.

The first Israeli soldiers who came to the site prayed with the settlers – an act for which the Israeli military said they would be disciplined.

An attempt by Israeli security forces to dislodge the settlers on Wednesday led to confrontations with a bigger group.

Palestinian security camera video shared with the BBC showed confrontations between Israeli soldiers and border police and a large crowd of settlers. The security forces used tear gas and stun grenades.

It is not clear exactly what the settlers in Qusra want. In the past, settlers have forced Palestinians out of their homes and seized their properties.

Their stated aim is to empty the area of its Palestinian residents.

Settlements are illegal under international law, but the Israeli government has promoted their recent rapid expansion.

The case is the latest to draw attention to the relative impunity of settlers and how Israeli forces are struggling to deal with rising settler violence.

Since January 2023, 127 Palestinian communities in the occupied West Bank have experienced full or partial displacement, including 47 that have been entirely displaced, affecting more than 6,390 Palestinians, the UN says.

It has registered that in 2026, about 3,800 Palestinians have been displaced due to settler violence, demolitions and evictions - nearly half of them children.

articles.title: Luigi Mangione pleads guilty to causing UnitedHealthcare CEO’s death in federal case
articles.excerpt:
Plea comes weeks before separate case is scheduled to start in New York, and could throw proceedings into disarray

Luigi Mangione pleaded guilty on Friday in a federal case in relation to the killing...
articles.body_text:
Plea comes weeks before separate case is scheduled to start in New York, and could throw proceedings into disarray

Luigi Mangione pleaded guilty on Friday in a federal case in relation to the killing of UnitedHealthcare executive Brian Thompson in 2024.

Mangione confessed that he shot and killed Thompson outside a New York City hotel on 4 December 2024. In his federal case, he faced stalking charges, after other charges, including murder, were dropped.

“I shot Mr Thompson in Manhattan and he died,” Mangione said towards the end of a hastily scheduled, 45-minute hearing. He added: “I knew what I was doing was illegal” but did not say that what he did was wrong or that he had any regrets.

The judge, Margaret Garnett, scheduled his sentencing for 18 December. Mangione’s federal trial had been due to begin next month but will not now happen, while state charges against him were still in the balance on Friday afternoon.

In the separate state case, Manhattan prosecutors have charged Mangione with murder and weapons counts and his state trial is scheduled for next 8 September. He had previously pleaded not guilty in both cases.

Within minutes of the guilty plea to stalking charges in the federal case and his admissions in court, Mangione’s defense lawyer, Karen Friedman Agnifilo, said she had filed a motion to dismiss the state murder case against him. Federal prosecutor Jamie McDonald told the court the government would seek life imprisonment for the killer.

Maryland-born Mangione, 28, came into court on Friday morning in beige jail scrubs with his wrists and ankles shackled, a change from recent appearances where he was in a jacket and shirt. He had been brought to the Manhattan courthouse from custody in Brooklyn. Relatives of Thompson were in court in a rare occurrence, sitting in the front row, and some of the family members began crying as Mangione told the judge what he had done.

In a federal case like this, the victim’s family has to agree to a plea deal by the defendant if such a deal is favored, avoiding a trial.

Among the relatives in court was Brian Thompson’s widow, Paulette Thompson, who was breathing heavily and grasping a loved one’s arm as Mangione described shooting her husband on a busy city sidewalk. Other family members held each other’s hands.

Mangione told the court that “after years of enduring severe back pain, a broken back, [and] navigating the obstacles of the health system”, he learned that UnitedHealthcare would be holding its annual investor conference in December 2024.

The location was not public but he traveled to New York City and emailed UnitedHealthcare leadership, posing as an institutional investor, to get more information, getting a response within an hour.

He also researched who would be attending. Mangione then said he printed a gun with a 3-D printer and affixed it with a silencer. “I shot Mr Thompson in Manhattan and he died,” he said. “When I did so, I understood that my actions would place him in fear of death or serious bodily injury. I knew what I was doing was illegal.”

The judge said earlier that Mangione was in a fit state to plead. He was asked a series of questions.

Mangione’s case has drawn extensive global attention as Thompson’s death spurred intense discussion about the US’s heavily criticized for-profit healthcare system. The attention has also been fueled by Mangione’s rise to virtual folk-hero status among some of his supporters, although there were almost none of the most vocal fans, dubbed “Mangionistas” outside the courthouse on Friday, as there had been for previous hearings.

Mangione’s decision to plead guilty in the federal trial came after days of intense speculation that his case would resolve before a trial. Mere hours after a final pre-trial conference in his state case, federal prosecutors and his defense had submitted a joint letter requesting a proceeding.

The shock plea came weeks before his Manhattan murder case was scheduled to start in state court and could throw those proceedings into disarray, as New York double jeopardy law could bar his state-level prosecution due to this plea.

Under New York state law, “a person may not be twice prosecuted for the same offense” and “a person may not be separately prosecuted for two offenses based upon the same act or criminal transaction”. A state appeals court decision points out, however, that these statements precede the word “unless” as well as a list of exceptions.

Mangione was arrested at an Altoona, Pennsylvania, McDonald’s on 9 December 2024 after a dramatic manhunt to find Thompson’s killer. Mangione in April 2025 pleaded not guilty to federal charges that he stalked and murdered Thompson.

Not long after Mangione’s arrest, Pam Bondi, then the US attorney general, announced that she would instruct prosecutors to seek the death penalty. She said that Thompson’s killing was a “premeditated, cold-blooded assassination that shocked America”.

Bondi also said that her position was aligned with “Trump’s agenda to stop violent crime and Make America Safe Again”.

But Judge Garnett on 30 January threw out two of the four counts in Mangione’s federal indictment including the death penalty-eligible charge of murder through use of a firearm, meaning this punishment was off the table. Garnett said that US supreme court precedents made the murder charge “incompatible” with the two stalking charges.

“This case will proceed to trial on counts one and two, which charge the defendant with causing Brian Thompson’s death under two federal stalking laws,” Garnett said in her order. “The potential maximum punishment for each of those offenses is life in prison without parole.

“Consequently, the chief practical effect of the legal infirmities of counts three and four, and this court’s decision that they must be dismissed, is solely to foreclose the death penalty as an available punishment to be considered by the jury that will otherwise determine, at trial, whether to convict the defendant for causing Brian Thompson’s death,” Garnett had said.

articles.title: UK diplomats no longer get hardship bonus for being posted to Buenos Aires
articles.excerpt:
Buenos Aires hosts the official workplace of the Argentinian president, shown here in front of Plaza de Mayo square

British diplomats in six locations around the world, including Buenos Aires and San...
articles.body_text:
Buenos Aires hosts the official workplace of the Argentinian president, shown here in front of Plaza de Mayo square

British diplomats in six locations around the world, including Buenos Aires and Santiago in South America, will no longer get hardship payments for working in dangerous cities.

Bonuses and respite breaks are granted to those working in cities considered risky, like Beirut in Lebanon, or with high crime, such as Pretoria in South Africa, or high air pollution in cities including New Delhi and Beijing.

The UK government has removed Santiago, in Chile, Panama City in Panama, Pyongyang in North Korea, Bamako in Mali, and Sarajevo in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in addition to the two south American cities, according to the latest list published last week, external.

The 144 locations still on the list include many trouble spots but also popular holiday destinations such as Bali and Rio De Janeiro, prompting criticism from the Conservatives.

Tory chairman­ Kevin Hollin­rake said civil servants receiving extra pay for working in such areas is unfair on the taxpayer.

The Foreign Office has given civil servants extra payments for working in areas where there is a high level of danger, or high risks to health, for the past 30 years.

They are meant to compensate staff and families for the additional costs and challenges of living overseas in difficult locations and are reviewed regularly.

Factors and risks covered by the allowance include security measures, climate, natural disaster, isolation and other impacts on quality of life.

Amounts are not routinely published but in 2009, the last time a breakdown was released, the highest payments for civil servants and their spouses were for postings to Karachi, Pakistan, which was worth an extra £26,647, or £14,804 in Abuja, the capital of Nigeria.

The hardship payment for being posted as part of a couple to Buenos Aires was £1,517 and Santiago was £777, according to the 2009 Diplomatic Services Allowances, external.

Answering a parliamentary question from Tory peer Lord Moylan, external, Foreign Office minister Lord Wood of Anfield said assessments of hardship take into account factors that mean members of staff are required to take additional breaks for the benefit of their physical or mental health.

He added: "These arrangements are not new, and indeed have applied consistently under successive governments for a number of decades."

Bangkok, Cape Town, and Kuala Lumpur are still among the cities that qualify for hardship payments, alongside Dubai, Abu Dhabi, and Muscat.

Hollinrake said it was unfair that taxpayers were "footing the bill" for these destinations and pledged to cut the size of the civil service if Conservatives were returned to power.

"Whilst businesses and families are paying higher taxes to fund this government's policies, civil servants are being sent on taxpayer-funded jollies to places like Bali, Cape Town and the Maldives," he said.

"This kind of nonsense has no place in government."

But the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office defended the scheme, with a spokesperson saying: "British diplomats serve their country around the globe, including in some of the toughest and most challenging physical and political environments in the world.

"We have a duty of care to ensure our staff are properly supported, and compensation and other provisions reflect the circumstances of the posting, as it would be in any private sector job."
