Country star Riley Green told Fox News Digital he won't abandon his Alabama farm even though he has "every reason" to move to Nashville.

Matthew McConaughey is a Texas boy at heart.

During Wednesday...
articles.body_text:
Country star Riley Green told Fox News Digital he won't abandon his Alabama farm even though he has "every reason" to move to Nashville.

Matthew McConaughey is a Texas boy at heart.

During Wednesday's episode of "The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon," the 56-year-old actor embraced his Southern roots by performing Ella Langley's hit song, "Choosin' Texas," alongside Fallon and indie folk band The Last Bison. The cover quickly drew attention on social media and even earned a response from Langley herself.

"I don't think I'll ever recover from this," Langley wrote on her Instagram Stories alongside a video of McConaughey and Fallon jamming to her hit song.

KOE WETZEL AND ELLA LANGLEY RELEASE NEW COUNTRY SONG 'JADED' AND IT'S ALREADY GOING VIRAL

Matthew McConaughey covered Ella Langley's "Choosin' Texas" during an appearance on "The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon." (Getty Images)

"POV me driving singing this with my whole chest," one fan commented.

"The cover we didn’t know we needed," another wrote.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

Host Jimmy Fallon and actor Matthew McConaughey appear during "Audience Suggestion Box" on Wednesday, Aug. 12, 2026. (Todd Owyoung/NBC via Getty Images)

The performance unfolded during a new installment of "Tonight Show Audience Suggestion Box," when Fallon read a submission that combined Langley’s hit with McConaughey’s latest movie, "The Rivals of Amziah King."

"I love that song ‘Choosin’ Texas’ by Ella Langley," Fallon read. "And I’m really excited to see Matthew McConaughey’s new movie ‘The Rivals of Amziah King,’ where he performs in a bluegrass band. If there was only a way to combine those things, that would be a dream come true."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"This is ‘The Tonight Show,’ where dreams become reality," Fallon quipped.

Moments later, the curtain opened to reveal McConaughey with a mandolin in hand alongside The Last Bison, while Fallon joined in on the washboard. The group then launched into a bluegrass rendition of Langley's chart-topping hit.

Matthew McConaughey is a Texas native.  (Getty Images)

McConaughey's cover comes as "Choosin' Texas" continues to make history for Langley.

ELLA LANGLEY'S 'CHOOSIN' TEXAS' SPENDS 15 WEEKS AT NUMBER ONE ON THE BILLBOARD HOT 100

The country anthem recently scored its 17th nonconsecutive week at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100, making it the longest-running non-holiday No. 1 by a solo female artist in the chart's history.

The milestone pushed Langley past Whitney Houston's "I Will Always Love You" and Mariah Carey's "We Belong Together," which each spent 14 weeks at the top of the chart.

For McConaughey, the song choice was particularly fitting.

The Oscar-winning actor has long been outspoken about his love for the Lone Star State, where he was born and later returned to raise his family.

‘SOPRANOS’ STAR JAMIE-LYNN SIGLER FLED HOLLYWOOD FOR TEXAS WHERE SHE NO LONGER FEELS ‘WATCHED’

McConaughey left Malibu, California, for Austin, Texas, with his wife, Camila Alves McConaughey, and their three children in 2014. He previously explained that returning to Texas was always part of his plan once he started a family.

McConaughey and his wife, Camila Alves, share three children together.  (Rick Kern/Getty Images)

"This has always been home, there are multiple reasons for that," McConaughey previously said during an appearance on "Today."

The "Dallas Buyers Club" star said his mother and two older brothers were also in Texas and explained that he wanted his children to experience some of the same values he grew up around.

"I wanted them to have what I grew up around," he said, adding that there is a certain amount of "common sense" that comes with life in Texas.

Christina Dugan Ramirez is an entertainment journalist with more than 15 years of experience, including a decade at PEOPLE writing high-profile cover stories, covering Hollywood's biggest events, and interviewing many of the industry's most influential stars before joining Fox News Digital in 2024.

articles.title: Ukraine ‘offering Russia deal to halt attacks on civilian ships in Black Sea’
articles.excerpt:
Kyiv reportedly suggested mutual agreement in attempt to reopen crucial grain corridor

Ukraine has proposed a deal with Russia for both sides to halt their attacks on civilian ships in the Black Sea ...
articles.body_text:
Kyiv reportedly suggested mutual agreement in attempt to reopen crucial grain corridor

Ukraine has proposed a deal with Russia for both sides to halt their attacks on civilian ships in the Black Sea in an apparent attempt to reopen a crucial grain corridor, Reuters reports.

Kyiv is said to have made the offer through a third party. Moscow has yet to respond, the news agency added. The busy waterway is a key export route for both Russia and Ukraine, used to transport grain and other vital foodstuffs worldwide.

Since July Ukraine has effectively closed the route for commercial Russian shipping. Its drones have hit nearly 220 vessels in the Sea of Azov and Black Sea, including oil tankers, grain cargo ships and passenger ferries.

The campaign has forced Russia to suspend shipping through a canal that connects the Caspian Sea with the Sea of Azov via a Russian river network. The route goes through the Kerch strait between occupied Crimea and Russia, and leads on to the Bosphorus strait in Turkey.

During the same period, Russia has escalated its attacks on Ukraine’s southern ports, dealing a severe blow to the country’s agricultural sector. About 90% of grain and sunflower shipments leave from Odesa, and the neighbouring harbours of Chornomorsk and Pivdenne.

In July Russian drones killed 10 sailors soon after their Turkish-owned grain carrier, the Golden Leo, set off from Odesa. Many of the victims were from Syria and India. Another 16 port workers and sailors have died in other recent strikes.

Kyiv’s reported overture appears to be pragmatic, allowing both sides to resume shipments that are crucial to international food security. It comes as the country’s harvest season begins and with shipping from Ukrainian ports at a virtual standstill.

The offer also follows a report in the FT that the US vice-president, JD Vance, had asked Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy to cease some attacks on the Russian Black Sea port of Novorossiysk.

In a phone call on 31 July, Vance complained that Ukrainian strikes on tankers carrying oil from Kazakhstan were hurting US companies and destabilising oil prices. He told Zelenskyy to stop them, the newspaper said, citing unnamed Ukrainian officials.

Zelenskyy’s office has not commented, but Kyiv is in the middle of delicate negotiations with the Trump administration. It is seeking US-manufactured Patriot interceptors to defend Ukrainian cities from rampant Russian ballistic missile and drone swarms.

Since the phone call, Ukraine’s unmanned systems forces have not attacked ships carrying oil from Kazakhstan via the Caspian Pipeline Consortium terminal. But they have continued to pound other targets in Novorossiysk, which is home to Russia’s Black Sea naval fleet.

On Wednesday Zelenskyy hailed a “massive” combined attack on the port, featuring rockets, jets and sea drones. He said Ukraine had taken out Russian warships, including two frigates, a large landing ship, a corvette and other vessels. They had been “hiding” in Novorossiysk Bay, he wrote on Telegram.

Other targets included two major grain export terminals, it was reported. Russian officials said three people, including a child, were killed. “It is entirely justified that Ukraine is responding to Russia’s war, and it is Russia that can and must bring this war to an end,” Zelenskyy posted.

The two sides have previously signed an agreement, brokered by Turkey and the UN, to stop maritime attacks. The Black Sea grain initiative lasted from July 2022 to July 2023. It ended when the Kremlin refused to renew it, complaining that western sanctions were damaging Russia’s agricultural sector.

Ukraine subsequently reopened the route unilaterally, using sea drones to sink Russian ships using the north-west part of the Black Sea. Most vessels in Russia’s Black Sea fleet were forced to relocate from the exposed occupied Crimean port of Sevastopol to Novorossiysk.

articles.title: Bride serves McDonald's customer in wedding dress while tying knot at restaurant: 'Handing out extra sauces'
articles.excerpt: Jamie Callicoat tells Fox News Digital how she ended up celebrating her marriage to George Callicoat at the Akron, Ohio, restaurant where they work and even helped a customer while still wearing her w...
articles.body_text:
Jamie Callicoat tells Fox News Digital how she ended up celebrating her marriage to George Callicoat at the Akron, Ohio, restaurant where they work and even helped a customer while still wearing her wedding dress.

A Northeast Ohio McDonald's restaurant was transformed into a wedding venue last Saturday as two co-workers said "I do" in front of friends, family, fellow employees and the occasional customer.

"We had people trying to come in the lobby the whole time," despite the dining room being closed to the public for the ceremony and reception, bride Jamie Callicoat, of Akron, Ohio, told Fox News Digital this week after marrying co-worker George Callicoat.

"I was handing out extra sauces to an actual customer in my wedding dress."

'MCDONALD'S CHANGED THE COURSE OF MY LIFE': CONGRESSMAN SELLS BUSINESS HE BUILT SINCE HIS TEEN YEARS

Some customers made it to the kiosks inside to order, and the drive-thru remained open throughout the celebration. Everyone — including unsuspecting customers — "rolled with the punches," Jamie said.

"It's still work, if you're there off the clock, on the clock, whatever," she said. "We were there interrupting to have our personal wedding."

George and Jamie Callicoat pose with members of their wedding party outside the McDonald's where they work and were married. (Jamie Callicoat)

The intimate ceremony has since gone viral online.

"Social media content surrounding the wedding has already generated more than 20 million impressions across Instagram and Facebook, with the story continuing to spread," McDonald's of Northeast Ohio said in a news release.

MCDONALD'S NEWEST MENU ITEM HAS FANS BEGGING FOR ONE DISCONTINUED FAVORITE

"We kind of figured it would get some attention, but this is just unreal," Jamie said of the reaction.

The newlyweds were back at work on the Tuesday after their wedding as customers and others who frequent the restaurant began congratulating them.

"Our co-workers are amazing, our bosses are amazing and McDonald's is amazing for allowing us to do this."

"Our Brinks guys, who come and pick up our money, came in and they both walked right up to us and said, 'Oh my gosh, we've seen the video. Congratulations!'" Jamie said.

Jamie is a manager at the McDonald's where she wed George, the restaurant's crew trainer.

McDonald's provided the venue and helped decorate the restaurant. (Jamie Callicoat)

The pair met through mutual friends at Cedar Point in Ohio in June 2025 and went on a few dates. When Jamie moved to Akron and began working at the McDonald's in October 2025, George trained her.

Jamie said George's personality drew her to him.

"We just get along very well," she said. "I love everything about George. He's a great guy."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"I love everything about her," George told Fox News Digital. "She is a wonderful person, very caring, very kind."

The pair became engaged at Cedar Point and initially planned to get married there, too. Then a district manager jokingly suggested they tie the knot at the McDonald's where they both work.

"We thought about it for a day or so and went back and were like, 'Well, were you guys serious?'" Jamie recalled. "And one thing kind of led to another, and here we are."

Jamie Callicoat said her bosses planted the idea of getting married inside the McDonald's. (Dana Dershaw)

The celebration became a team effort, McDonald's said in its news release.

"Crew members and managers came together to help make the couple's wedding day special, providing dinner, a wedding cake and other touches for the celebration," McDonald's said. "Even the officiant had a McDonald's connection: the husband of the restaurant's general manager performed the ceremony."

McDonald's provided the venue, and despite ultimately holding a larger celebration than the destination-style wedding they had originally envisioned, Jamie said the ceremony was "cost-effective."

The couple handled some of the decorations and food themselves. Guests were served pulled barbecue chicken, buffalo chicken dip, homemade rigatoni and fried chicken, while the kids ate fresh McDonald's food.

Even the flower girl got a McDonald's touch, tossing petals from a Happy Meal box.

"That was my decision, mostly," Jamie said. "I mean, we work at McDonald's. I thought it was cute."

George Callicoat trained his future bride when she started working at the McDonald's restaurant in Akron, Ohio. The husband of the location's general manager officiated the wedding ceremony. (Dana Dershaw)

The official Instagram account for McDonald's commented on a video of the ceremony, writing, "A modern day love story."

"Congrats to them on their McMarriage!" wrote another well-wisher. "'Forever After All' and we're McLovin' it."

One commenter even joked about McDonald's notoriously finicky soft-serve machines, but George said theirs wasn't a problem.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"Ours is always working, unless it's being cleaned," he said.

Tammy Snider, the location's general manager, said it was "so much more than a wedding at a McDonald's."

"It's a story about two people in love and a restaurant team that wanted to make sure they felt celebrated," Snider said. "Our restaurants are places where friendships are made, milestones are celebrated and communities come together. George and Jamie's wedding is such a beautiful example of that."

"We had a great time," she said. "Our co-workers are amazing, our bosses are amazing and McDonald's is amazing for allowing us to do this."

Teresa Mull is a freelance writer with the Lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Jack Story skipped his high school graduation to go bass fishing and walked away with $100K
articles.excerpt: Marine Veteran Matt Moore, owner of Hellbender Outfitters, builds custom fishing rods for Gold Star families and veterans in Eastern Tennessee. Moore shares his personal journey, revealing how nature ...
articles.body_text:
Marine Veteran Matt Moore, owner of Hellbender Outfitters, builds custom fishing rods for Gold Star families and veterans in Eastern Tennessee. Moore shares his personal journey, revealing how nature provided healing after military service. He emphasizes the importance of passing down durable fishing rods that tell a story, connecting individuals with the outdoors to support mental well-being and honor fallen heroes' families.

Jack Story didn’t walk across the stage at his high school graduation. He was too busy winning $100,000.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

The 18-year-old Georgia angler made the decision earlier this year to skip his graduation ceremony and compete in the Phoenix Bass Fishing League All-American on Lake Murray. Looking back now, it doesn’t sound like he lost much sleep over it.

Jack Story, 18, skipped his high school graduation and became the youngest-ever winner of the 43rd annual Phoenix Bass Fishing League (BFL) All-American Championship. (Photo courtesy of Jack Story)

During a recent interview with OutKick Outdoors, Story said he originally qualified through a regional tournament and "never really expected" to make it to the All-American. But once he found out the tournament landed on the same day as graduation, the choice was pretty simple.

"I was going fishing, and they could either be accommodating or not," Story said. "Thankfully, they were very helpful with it."

His school wasn’t completely thrilled, though. Story said the headmaster and others at the school "handled it about as well as they could have," even if they would have preferred to see him in a cap and gown.

Still, some tried to make him reconsider.

"One of my teachers kind of hinted that I should be at graduation," Story said. "But it just wasn’t even an option."

Watch Jack Story's full interview with OutKick Outdoors here:

Story went on to win the All-American and the $100,000 prize that came with it. He also qualified for REDCREST 2027 and the Toyota Series Championship — a pretty strong consolation prize for missing a graduation ceremony.

Still, even weeks later, he said the whole thing feels surreal.

"It was so stressful during the tournament that I think it was a huge relief, but I also didn’t even know what to do," Story said. "The feeling of accomplishment doesn’t even register. Looking back on it, it doesn’t feel real."

The win also came with a little family bragging rights.

Story’s dad previously fished the All-American and finished 34th. So yes, beating him was somewhere on the checklist.

"I thought that was going to be pretty easy given the lake it was on," Story said.

A 7 pound largemouth bass is held against a backdrop of cypress trees. (Getty: JLFCapture)

But that wasn’t the only goal. Story said he wanted to beat the other two anglers from his regional and keep advancing. Instead, he ended up winning the whole thing.

His dad’s advice has always been simple: If you’re going to do something, go all in. That applied to fishing, too.

"If I wanted to skip school to go fish, I was at least going to actually fish," Story said. "His thing was, if you’re going to fish, you’re going to fish all day. Just dedicate yourself to it."

That mindset mattered at Lake Murray. Because Story’s victory was anything but smooth.

The final day came down to 10 ounces, and Story said he knew it was going to be close. What made it worse was the fact that he had already been hit with penalties after issues with his livewells and oxygen tank.

"I was really stressed out about the fact that I could lose because of penalties," Story said. "I’d rather lose by 10 pounds than lose by any sort of penalty."

In other words, this was not some easy stroll to a giant check.

DENNY HAMLIN CHASES MONSTER LARGEMOUTH BASS IN TEXAS WITH BASSMASTER PRO CHRIS ZALDAIN

There was also the added pressure of chasing history. Now the tournament's youngest winner ever, Story broke a 15-year record previously held by Jacob Wheeler — one of the biggest names in the sport.

Unfortunately, Story found out about the record before the tournament was over.

"I honestly wish I would have figured that out after, rather than the night of day two," Story said. "Somebody texted me, and I was like, ‘Dude, that is not what I needed.’ It made it more stressful because instantly, that became my goal."

Since the win, Story said life has included more interviews, podcasts and attention. But mostly, it has included more fishing.

He had a rough finish in a high school tournament shortly after the All-American, and that did not sit well with him.

"I hate losing in fishing, especially when it’s to one of my friends," Story said. "I’ve got to get my get-back, if that makes sense. I want to go beat them again the next day. I just want to fish, and I want to win."

Story is headed to Carson-Newman, where he plans to fish in college. He is also considering fishing the Tackle Warehouse Invitationals if he can make the schedule work.

For other kids who want to get into competitive fishing, Story said persistence matters. So does helping parents understand that fishing can create real opportunities, including scholarships.

"I don’t think people really realize that you can get a scholarship for fishing," Story said. "If you dedicate yourself and put in the constructive work to get there, I think it’s easier than people make it seem. You just have to know how to do it."

A fisherman holds a fishing rod by a lake during sunset in an outdoor setting. (scyther5 / Getty Images)

More than that, Story said fishing gave him something positive to pour himself into.

"I’m out of trouble because I fish," he said. "It keeps you out of trouble. You’re doing something outdoors. It’s good."

And even after winning $100,000 at 18 years old, Story is already thinking about helping more kids get on the water.

STAY "FEARLESS" ON THE GO! TAKE TOMI LAHREN WITH YOU. DOWNLOAD THE TLIF PODCAST NOW!

"I really enjoy taking the younger generation fishing," Story said. "I think every kid deserves the opportunity to fish, and that’s that."

Love all things fishing and outdoors? Follow OutKick Outdoors on Instagram and TikTok!

articles.title: Conditions on US aircraft carrier at sea for more than 250 days raise alarms
articles.excerpt: Concern about living conditions on a US aircraft carrier that has been deployed in the Middle East for more than 250 days is leading a US senator to demand answers from the military about the vessel a...
articles.body_text:
Concern about living conditions on a US aircraft carrier that has been deployed in the Middle East for more than 250 days is leading a US senator to demand answers from the military about the vessel and putting more pressure on the Trump administration over the Iran war.

Reports suggest US military members aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln are living with food shortages and broken plumbing and that there have been suicide attempts.

Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth on Thursday called the reports "completely misrepresented".

The carrier left San Diego in November for the South China Sea and was then sent to the Middle East ahead of the attacks on Iran in February. No return date has been announced.

Connecticut Senator Richard Blumenthal, a Democrat, listed the reported hardships on the carrier,  where about 5,000 people are on board, in a letter to Hegseth:  "Shortages of basic supplies, water contamination, plumbing issues, deteriorating mental health, deck safety concerns, and disruptions in the mail system, which have caused many care packages in route to the ship to be lost in transit for months."

"These reports warrant immediate attention," he wrote, "but they also raise a broader question: whether the Navy can sustain the operational tempo now being demanded of its carrier force."

The Military Times and Stars and Stripes reported on Tuesday that multiple sailors on the carrier had considered suicide or attempted to jump overboard, according to their family members.

CBS News, the BBC's US partner, has reported that last month a sailor went overboard and was recovered safely, citing two unnamed officials. The circumstances are currently under investigation.

The deployment was originally set to end in May, but has been repeatedly extended with no date publicly announced for when the carrier will return.

Hegseth, while speaking to reporters in Panama on Thursday, said the government makes sure "every ship, every crew, every captain has everything we can provide them at every single moment".

"Some deployments are longer than others, and I have more respect and gratitude for those sailors than anybody," he sid. "What they do in those high seas in those austere conditions with less port calls - it's incredible."

On Thursday, the Wall Street Journal reported that the US is preparing to replace the Lincoln with the aircraft carrier USS George Washington as part of a previously scheduled rotation plan. The BBC has contacted the Pentagon about the report.

Laysla De Oliveira and Jill Wagner told Fox News Digital how the third season of Taylor Sheridan's hit series will be different from the rest.

"Lioness" star Michael Kelly is a huge fan of Taylor Sheridan.

The third season of Sheridan's Paramount+ CIA/military series is currently airing, and as expected, it's absolutely awesome.

Of course, that's far from Sheridan's only monster hit. He's responsible for creating the "Yellowstone" universe, "Sicario," "Landman," "Wind River" and many other exceptional projects.

ZOE SALDAÑA SAYS TAYLOR SHERIDAN 'REALLY SEES WOMEN' AS LIONESS SEASON THREE HITS PARAMOUNT+

Taylor Sheridan attends the black carpet event for the "Yellowstone" Season 5 Fort Worth premiere at Hotel Drover on Nov. 13, 2022, in Fort Worth, Texas. (Omar Vega/Getty Images)

Kelly is one of the major figures in "Lioness," and it sounds like he'll do literally any project Sheridan might cook up.

The talented actor told ScreenRant the following when discussing the creative visionary:

I've never thought about how the shows could cross over, but I have told Taylor, I'm like, 'Bro, anything you ever want me to do, I'll do. I love being in Texas. I love saying your words.' I think he's truly a standalone talent. There's nobody who's doing or has ever done what he's doing. It's incredible what he does. And he's just one of the smartest dudes you'll ever meet. He's fricking brilliant, man. Brilliant. And just one of the greatest storytellers.

TAYLOR SHERIDAN’S 'YELLOWSTONE’ FORMULA TURNS COUNTRY STARS INTO SCENE-STEALERS AS MORGAN WADE MAKES HER DEBUT

Jessalyn Gilsig as FBI Dir. Francine Wexler, Bruce McGill as Monty Holler, Morgan Freeman as Edwin Mullins, Michael Kelly as Byron Westfield, Nicole Kidman as Kaitlyn and Zoe Saldaña as Joe appear in episode 2 of season 3 of Lioness, streaming on Paramount+. (Lauren Smith/Paramount+)

He's worked with Kevin Costner, Sam Elliott, Zoe Saldaña, Nicole Kidman, Morgan Freeman, Jeremy Renner, Billy Bob Thornton and more.

Getting into a Sheridan project is about the biggest thing you can do in the entertainment world in 2026, and it all started with "Yellowstone."

Air India is to test all of its pilots for banned substances, starting immediately.

It comes after an incident las...
articles.body_text:
The airline said in a memo that the move would reassure passengers and stakeholders

Air India is to test all of its pilots for banned substances, starting immediately.

It comes after an incident last week in which its Phuket to Delhi flight suddenly lost altitude, with a preliminary report saying the senior pilot had to retake their substance test. Reports say they had tested positive for marijuana.

Pilots at the airline's budget arm, Air India Express, will also be subject to the tests from Thursday.

Existing rules require at least 10% of pilots to be tested at random.

Seventeen passengers and crew were injured when the Airbus lost about 91 metres (300 feet) in height shortly after departure on 4 August.

It is being investigated by Indian authorities working alongside Airbus and France's air safety agency.

Both pilots of the flight have been removed from duties until the investigation is complete.

In a memo seen by the BBC, Air India said it was "important to go further" in its testing.

"This initiative, which goes beyond regulatory requirements, reflects our determination to uphold the highest standards of safety and professionalism, and to provide reassurance to our passengers, stakeholders and the community at large," it said.

The airline has already been under scrutiny after a June 2025 flight from Ahmedabad to London crashed shortly after take-off, killing 241 people on board and 19 on the ground. Only one passenger survived.

The tests - for substances as well as medications prohibited under aviation regulations - are being carried out alongside training sessions at Air India's academy, as well as other locations including briefing centres and offices.

Last week, former Ethiopian Airlines boss Tewolde Gebremariam became Air India's new chief executive.

articles.title: Mark Consuelos confesses what would keep him in 'loveless marriage' with Kelly Ripa

articles.body_text:
Dana Perino discusses the anticipated Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce wedding, offering her perspective on marriage. She stresses that happiness in a marriage is built on mutual trust rather than extravagant costs or prenups. Perino emphasizes a commitment-first approach for couples considering long-term unions.

Mark Consuelos revealed that he’d rather stay in a "loveless marriage" with Kelly Ripa than risk losing their dog Lena in a divorce.

"How do we fight over pets in a divorce?" Ripa asked in the opening segment of Tuesday's episode of "Live with Kelly and Mark," a prerecorded episode from before she was out for oral surgery.

"I mean, listen. Let’s just put it this way," Consuelos responded. "I would stay in a loveless marriage just to make sure I could be with Lena every day. That’s how much I love Lena."

KELLY RIPA'S PAINFUL SURGERY LEAVES HER UNABLE TO SPEAK

Mark Consuelos joked that he would rather stay in a "loveless marriage" than risk losing their dog, Lena. (FilmMagic)

Ripa asked him sarcastically, "Is that all you’re asking for is a loveless marriage? Because that can be arranged."

Consuelos added that if he ever lost Lena in a divorce, he would "stay up at night, wondering what she is doing."

Ripa quipped that he would be "wondering if there was some other man petting her."

They were discussing a new bill in Pennsylvania that would change pets from being considered property to members of the family in a divorce, according to People.

The couple rescued Lena, a Maltese and Shih Tzu mix, in 2021 after she was featured in a pet adoption segment on the show.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Mark Consuelos is seen balancing his dog, Lena, on his head. (Kelly Ripa/Instagram)

Ripa said her main worry when she adopted Lena was that she wouldn’t get along with Chewie, a Shih Tzu she adopted from a 2007 segment on the show.

The two dogs got along right away, she said — but her children wanted Lena to be named after a "Star Wars" character.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

"My kids want her to be named Leia, as in Princess Leia, because we have Chewie," she said on the show soon after adopting the pup, according to People. "I don't know. I need guidance."

Kelly Ripa and Mark Consuelos have been married since 1996. (Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)

Ripa talked about the importance of rescuing pets on the show in 2022.

"Adopt your dogs if you can, because they’re the best," she said to applause from the audience. "They’re like, ‘We’ve been in the system, we don’t want to go back. We’re going to be extra good. We’re hardly going to poop anywhere we’re not supposed to, and we’re rarely going to chew things that aren’t meant to be chewed.'"

Ripa and Consuelos have been married for 30 years and they share three children.

Brie Stimson is a Los Angeles-based entertainment and breaking news writer for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Mangione lawyers to meet federal prosecutors amid reports of plea deal
articles.excerpt: Attorneys for Luigi Mangione, who is accused of killing United Healthcare CEO Brian Thompson in New York in 2024, are meeting federal prosecutors on Friday amid US media reports about a potential plea...
articles.body_text:
Attorneys for Luigi Mangione, who is accused of killing United Healthcare CEO Brian Thompson in New York in 2024, are meeting federal prosecutors on Friday amid US media reports about a potential plea agreement.

Mangione faces two federal stalking crimes that carry a maximum penalty of life in prison without parole, but it was not immediately clear which charges are under discussion.

"There's a conference scheduled for 11 am on Friday, and that's all we can say at this time," Jamie McDonald, the US Attorney for the Southern District of New York (SDNY), said this week.

Mangione also faces a separate state trial in the case. He has pleaded not guilty to all charges in both cases.

Discussion of a plea deal does not guarantee one will be reached, and such arrangements can fall apart. Any deal must also be approved by the court.

Federal prosecutors brought the stalking charges against Mangione for allegedly travelling, and using surveillance, to kill Thompson.

A federal judge threw out two other charges in January, one of which carried the death penalty as a possible sentence.

Mangione's attorneys, the SDNY, and Manhattan District Attorney's office did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.

His attorneys have previously argued he should not be tried in both state and federal court. At the moment, the judges presiding over both cases have allowed the trials to proceed.

But if Mangione pleads guilty in his federal case, it could open the door for his attorneys to argue the state case runs afoul of double jeopardy – a constitutional protection that prevents an individual from being prosecuted twice for the same crime.

New York's state constitution has its own prohibition on double jeopardy, which, if invoked here, could have a knock-on effect on Mangione's upcoming state trial.

"If a federal prosecution has been completed on a matter, the state cannot prosecute the matter on those same facts," said Mitchell Epner, a white-collar attorney and former federal prosecutor.

Mangione's state trial is scheduled to begin on 8 September, while the federal trial is listed for January 2027.

articles.title: Reports of US sailors in Middle East trying to jump ship spark outcry
articles.excerpt: Lawmakers in the United States have raised the alarm over reports of dire conditions on an aircraft carrier deployed to the Middle East amid the US-Israel war with Iran, including accounts of sailors ...
articles.body_text:
Lawmakers in the United States have raised the alarm over reports of dire conditions on an aircraft carrier deployed to the Middle East amid the US-Israel war with Iran, including accounts of sailors trying to jump overboard.

The response has included a direct appeal to Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth, asking for further information about conditions on board the USS Abraham Lincoln and demanding that a bipartisan congressional delegation be allowed to visit the ship.

In a letter to Hegseth, Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal noted that the aircraft carrier, with more than 5,000 US sailors and Marines, has been “continuously at sea for a record length of nearly seven months”. That surpasses any previous deployment of a US aircraft carrier without a port stop.

Blumenthal noted that the vessel’s mission was meant to end in May but has been repeatedly extended amid the war on Iran. The conflict remains in a state of grinding limbo, with a memorandum of understanding to end the fighting largely defunct and further diplomatic efforts stalled.

He pointed to reports of deteriorating mental health on board, as well as shortages of basic supplies, water contamination, an increase in safety incidents, and even disruptions to mail services, through which those on board receive care packages.

“These reports warrant immediate attention, but they also raise a broader question: whether the Navy can sustain the operational tempo now being demanded of its carrier force, particularly as this administration repeatedly commits US forces to conflicts of its own choosing and increasingly relies on aircraft carriers to sustain those operations,” Blumenthal wrote.

In a list of questions, the senator asked for a clear end date for the mission, how the navy is measuring mental health metrics, and how the deployment fits into broader goals.

Senator Ruben Gallego, also a Democrat, went further, saying the navy “must allow a bipartisan Congressional Delegation to visit the USS Lincoln to conduct an oversight investigation into this horrible situation”.

Such delegations, said Gallego, “have visited war zones to inspect the conditions of our troops. There is no reason to be denied access.”

Senator Mark Kelly, a former naval officer and astronaut, also called the reports of sailors attempting to jump into the sea “disturbing”.

“Long deployments are hard. They are a lot harder when the mission isn’t well defined and there is no end in sight,” he said in a post on X, along with a link to military mental health resources.

The increased attention on the USS Abraham Lincoln comes amid two reports by the Navy Times and Stars and Stripes, two publications that closely follow military affairs.

They cited several family members of military personnel on the vessel who reported declining mental health and morale, and cases of suicidal ideation from loved ones.

The Navy Times spoke on the record with the wife of one sailor, identified as Annabelle Loma, who said he had attempted to jump overboard amid what she described as severe burnout.

Another woman, identified as Maria Rodriguez, said her husband told her he had intervened in a separate instance of a shipmate “preparing to go overboard”.

Stars and Stripes said the issue was raised during a town hall meeting last week with acting secretary of the navy, Hung Cao, in San Diego, from where the USS Lincoln had last departed in November 2025.

On Thursday, CNN reported a sailor went overboard last month and was quickly rescued. The report, citing a US official, said the circumstances of the incident were not clear.

The navy did not immediately respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment. However, it told Stars and Stripes its “leadership is continuously conducting assessments to monitor and sustain the psychological readiness of every sailor”.

articles.title: Joey Chestnut suffers shocking defeat at minor league baseball game but it comes with one giant asterisk
articles.excerpt: Chowdown champ Joey "Jaws" Chestnut celebrates after winning the the Nathan's Famous Fourth of July International Hot Dog-Eating Contest in Coney Island's Maimonides Park on Sunday, July 4, 2021, in t...
articles.body_text:
Chowdown champ Joey "Jaws" Chestnut celebrates after winning the the Nathan's Famous Fourth of July International Hot Dog-Eating Contest in Coney Island's Maimonides Park on Sunday, July 4, 2021, in the Brooklyn borough of New York. (AP Photo/Brittainy Newman)

I've said it many times, unironically: Joey Chestnut is one of, if not the most dominant athletes of all time.

But even Michael Jordan took a couple of losses in his day, and the man they call "Jaws" just took a heartbreaking loss in a tater tot eating contest during his barnstorming tour of minor league baseball stadiums.

However, this loss will come with one big, fat asterisk.

JOEY CHESTNUT REVEALS FOODS HE WON'T EAT IN COMPETITION AS HE TOURS MINOR LEAGUE STADIUMS FOR LOCAL DELICACIES

Competitive eating great Joey Chestnut suffered a shocking defeat in a tater tot eating contest in Wisconsin... or did he? (Photo by David Jensen/MLS via Getty Images)

Chestnut has been going around the country for special events and doing what he does best, eating copious amounts of food and obliterating the competition in the process.

However, when he rolled into a Lake Country DockHounds game just outside of Milwaukee, Chestnut met his match.

He lost the tater tot eating contest by just one tenth of an ounce.

A stunner. I can't even wrap my head around how much tater tot is equal to a tenth of an ounce. I wish I had a bag of Ore-Ida's and a kitchen scale on me to figure it out (I checked the freezer; no tots, but there was a freezer-burned bag of Arby's curly fries in the back, so we were close).

It has to be like a sliver of a tot. You could accidentally inhale that much and not even notice.

Joey Chestnut housed an ungodly number of Impossible chicken nuggets at a San Francisco Giants game last season. (Photo by Ezra Shaw/Getty Images)

Reread that post: Chestnut took on pairs of fans.

That means two guys tag-teamed trays of tots like a pair of hungry Napoleon Dynamites and still only won by less of a tater tot than is probably between your driver's seat and center console right now.

STAY "FEARLESS" ON THE GO! TAKE TOMI LAHREN WITH YOU. DOWNLOAD THE TLIF PODCAST NOW!

So you know what? That's not a loss for Chestnut; that's a win in my book, and the record books should reflect that.

Give him the L, but let's make sure that there's an asterisk on stand-by to explain it.

I knew there was no way Jaws was going down mano-a-mano in a tot-off.

articles.title: Train derailment in East Sussex closes several routes
articles.excerpt:
All passengers now off the train with no deaths or serious injuries reported, but Southern rail says there will be major disruption to services in area

A passenger train has derailed between Haywards...
articles.body_text:
All passengers now off the train with no deaths or serious injuries reported, but Southern rail says there will be major disruption to services in area

A passenger train has derailed between Haywards Heath and Lewes in East Sussex, prompting a rapid emergency response in the area.

Images of the aftermath show at least two carriages on their side. They appeared to show passengers standing on top of the toppled carriages while others could be seen in an area of heathland alongside emergency workers.

All passengers are now believed to be off the train and there are not believed to be any deaths or critical injuries. “There are no fatalities or serious injuries. Everyone is now off the train. It’s walking wounded basically,” a government source said.

Several rail routes were closed after the Southern service came off the tracks just before 4pm.

Emergency services said people should avoid the area, and that anyone travelling by rail in the area should allow up to 60 minutes extra for their journey.

A spokesperson for Network Rail and Southern Rail said: “We can confirm that the 1424 Southern passenger service from Victoria to Eastbourne has derailed in the Lewes area of East Sussex. Emergency services are on site and we will update with more information when we can. Trains through the area are suspended and passengers are advised to check online at southernrailway.com for the latest service information.”

A statement from British Transport Police said: “We’re responding alongside paramedics and the fire service and will provide more information as soon as we can.”

Heidi Alexander, the transport secretary, tweeted: “Deeply concerned of reports of a derailment involving a Southern train in Lewes, Sussex.

“Grateful to emergency services who are on the scene supporting those impacted. We are working quickly with the rail industry and local partners to assist passengers.”

Southern rail confirmed there would be major disruption to its services in the area.

In an update on X the operator said the derailment occurred between Haywards Heath and Lewes, meaning that there are currently no trains between Brighton and Lewes, Haywards Heath and Lewes and Seaford/Eastbourne and Lewes.

The company told passengers: “You should delay your journey in this area until later on today, or use an alternative route to travel.”

James MacCleary, the MP for Lewes, said: “I am aware of very concerning reports of a train crash in the Lewes area this afternoon.
 “I am in touch with the relevant authorities now and will provide further updates as soon as I have more information.
 “This is clearly a very serious and developing incident, and my thoughts are with everyone affected. In the meantime, if you are concerned about someone or need urgent assistance, please contact the emergency services.”

articles.title: Is Russia’s economy cracking despite the Iran war windfall?
articles.excerpt:
A widening deficit and Ukrainian strikes are testing Russia’s economy, even as war in the Middle East lifts oil revenue.

Russia’s economy has held up longer than many expected, defying Western sancti...
articles.body_text:
A widening deficit and Ukrainian strikes are testing Russia’s economy, even as war in the Middle East lifts oil revenue.

Russia’s economy has held up longer than many expected, defying Western sanctions.

But four years into the Russia-Ukraine war, the strain is starting to bite. Growth is forecast to slow to its weakest pace since 2022. The budget deficit is widening. And Ukrainian strikes are reaching deeper into the economy.

Even so, Moscow’s pockets remain deep, with more than $300bn in accessible reserves. The US-Israel war on Iran has handed it a windfall, sending energy prices higher and boosting Moscow’s revenues.

The United States has moved to cut that off, with the US Senate backing tariffs of up to 100 percent on Russian energy buyers.

articles.title: Justice Department slams 'politically motivated demands' of DC Council asking govs to remove National Guard
articles.excerpt:
Tamara Jachym, the mother of a Capitol Hill intern killed in Washington last summer says the National Guard deployment is "working" as D.C. homicides fall sharply.

The Justice Department slammed the ...
articles.body_text:
Tamara Jachym, the mother of a Capitol Hill intern killed in Washington last summer says the National Guard deployment is "working" as D.C. homicides fall sharply.

The Justice Department slammed the D.C. Council for its "politically motivated demands" and "impotent theatrics" after its members sent letters to governors asking them to recall their National Guard troops from the nation’s capital.

The development comes as FBI Director Kash Patel told Fox News Digital this week that "homicides in D.C. are down an incredible 44% from last year" when President Donald Trump’s administration launched the Safe and Beautiful initiative in Washington, D.C., which increased the federal law enforcement presence and deployed hundreds of federal agents and National Guard troops to combat crime.

"I am not surprised that your recent letter to state governors regarding the National Guard feigns ignorance of the historic public safety strides made in our Nation's capital since August 11, 2025," Assistant Attorney General Colin McDonald wrote in a letter addressed to the D.C. Council. "I am surprised and saddened, however, that you would show such callousness — instead of compassion and care — toward your constituents, who now live in a city with far less violence and fear thanks to the National Guard and the D.C. Safe and Beautiful Task Force."

"Let me be clear, your council has no power to demand that governors remove their brave men and women from serving in uniform in our Nation's capital. Your politically-motivated letter is impotent theatrics not worth the paper it's written on, and D.C. is a much safer place no matter what you say," McDonald added. "Because you refuse to speak the truth about the life-preserving work of the Task Force, the truth will speak for itself."

FBI TOUTS 6,000 ARRESTS, 44% HOMICIDE DROP ONE YEAR INTO TRUMP'S DC CRIME CRACKDOWN

FILE - Members of the Arkansas National Guard continue their patrol after carrying an elderly woman in a wheelchair down the steps to the train platform due to an out-of-service elevator at the Columbia Heights metro station on Monday, Aug. 10, 2026, in Washington. The D.C. Council came under fire after requesting governors remove their National Guard troops from Washington, D.C. (Rod Lamkey/AP)

The Justice Department said in a message on X that "This Department of Justice will not stand for these politically motivated demands."

"We will continue standing with @POTUS and the Make D.C. Safe and Beautiful Task Force to deliver historic results for the community — and for visitors from across the country and around the world to enjoy," it added.

Fox News Digital has reached out to representatives of D.C. Council members for comment.

The letters, co-signed by the D.C. Council members, were sent to the governors of Alabama, Alaska, Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Hawaii, Idaho, Indiana, Louisiana, Mississippi, Montana, Nebraska, Nevada, North Carolina, Oklahoma, Puerto Rico, South Carolina, Tennessee, West Virginia and Wyoming in late July, according to the office of Councilmember At-Large Robert White.

Each letter opened the same, saying, "We write as elected officials representing the District of Columbia to respectfully request that you withdraw all troops currently deployed to the District by September 1, 2026."

DC MURDER RATE SEES ASTONISHING TURNAROUND AS TRUMP TEAM CREDITS FEDERAL CRACKDOWN

Members of the National Guard walk on patrol as Free DC protesters rally against the continued National Guard presence in Washington on the one-year anniversary of President Trump's emergency declaration activating the Guard, Tuesday, Aug. 11, 2026. (Jacquelyn Martin/AP)

"There are approximately 5,148 Guard personnel currently deployed to the District under the premise that an extraordinary military presence was necessary to address public safety. Yet analysis of the deployment has found only a modest decrease in property crime and no measurable reduction in violent crime attributable to the Guard’s presence since August 2025," the letters continue.

"The deployment has, however, cost American taxpayers more than $3 million per day, according to the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office. Continuing this deployment despite the absence of a demonstrated violent-crime benefit would misuse both taxpayer dollars — in the billions, if maintained for years at its expanded scale — and the service of the Guard member themselves," the letters add, claiming that at a time where families in each of the states "and across the country are struggling with the cost of groceries, housing, health care, and other necessities, wasting those resources on an ineffective, indefinite deployment that neither District residents nor officials asked for is disrespectful to American taxpayers."

The letters conclude by saying that: "We recognize that the America 250 events present significant public safety and logistical challenges for the District and have required coordination across multiple jurisdictions. We are grateful to the Guard members who have been present to support the nation’s capital during this exceptionally busy period. Once the principal event-related needs conclude on September 1, 2026, we respectfully ask that they be permitted to return home to their families, careers and communities, rather than remain indefinitely assigned to a costly mission that has not demonstrated a measurable impact on violent crime."

However, McDonald said in his letter "Thanks to courageous and steadfast support from National Guard units, Task Force members have conducted thousands of arrests, located lost and missing children, and taken substantial numbers of illegal firearms off the city's streets" and that the National Guard "has personally intervened in numerous assaults and provided medical aid on innumerable occasions, including repeatedly administering life-saving NARCAN to citizens in peril."

FILE - National Guard members patrol the National Mall in Washington, DC, on Aug. 30, 2025. McDonald said Guard members repeatedly administered life-saving NARCAN to citizens in distress. (Andrew Leyden/Getty)

"While you slander these men and women as ‘outside military forces,’ I refer to them as true American heroes," he also said. "You should withdraw your letters and dedicate your remaining time in public service to correcting D.C.'s laws to ensure criminals are punished and the public is protected — not the other way around."

Fox News Digital’s Michael Sinkewicz contributed to this report.

Greg Norman is a reporter at Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Third person dies at New Jersey immigration detention center
articles.excerpt:
José Chajón-Raxón experienced ‘seizure-like activity’ at Delaney Hall and later died after being hospitalized

A Guatemalan immigrant detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) at a Newa...
articles.body_text:
José Chajón-Raxón experienced ‘seizure-like activity’ at Delaney Hall and later died after being hospitalized

A Guatemalan immigrant detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) at a Newark, New Jersey, facility suffered a medical emergency and later died after being hospitalized, according to the Trump administration.

José Chajón-Raxón is the third immigrant to die after being held at Delaney Hall, an ICE detention center that reopened in May 2025 amid the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.

A nurse responded when Chajón-Raxón experienced a medical emergency and “witnessed Chajón-Raxón experiencing seizure-like activity”, according to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). Medical personnel were called, and he was transported to a hospital, the DHS said in a statement shared with the Guardian.

ICE agents had arrested Chajón-Raxón before bringing him to Delaney Hall on 18 July, the agency said. Four days later, Chajón-Raxón was “released from ICE custody on July 22”, according to the agency, which did not provide further details about the circumstances of his release.

Key questions about what happened next remain unanswered in the DHS account. The department did not say what occurred after Chajón-Raxón arrived at the hospital, whether he left the hospital before his death or exactly when he died.

“Per ICE policy, when an individual is no longer in ICE custody then ICE will no longer be responsible for monitoring or reviewing deaths that may occur. This is common sense,” the DHS statement said.

The case comes after a policy shift announced earlier this year under which the agency stopped reporting deaths occurring within 30 days after a person is released from custody. That change reversed a policy put in place by the Biden administration in 2021.

US representative Rob Menendez, a New Jersey Democrat who has regularly visited Delaney Hall, has sharply criticized the change. Menendez told the Associated Press that it creates a “loophole” allowing the agency to release someone from custody and then “claim it has no responsibility to investigate their death or inform Congress and the public”.

Chajón-Raxón’s death did not become publicly known until Menendez disclosed it last week in the aftermath of another death connected to the facility.

Delaney Hall has already faced scrutiny from human rights advocates and Democrats over two other deaths involving immigrants detained there.

Edwin López-Cornejo, a man from El Salvador, died earlier this month after experiencing a medical emergency while in ICE detention. Jean Wilson Brutus, a Haitian man who had also been detained at Delaney Hall, died in December.

The latest disclosure adds to broader concerns surrounding deaths in immigration detention. More than 50 people have died in ICE custody nationwide since Donald Trump took office, while rights groups have repeatedly raised alarms about medical care and conditions inside detention facilities.

Delaney Hall itself has increasingly drawn national attention. In recent months, protests have followed allegations of problems including physical abuse by guards and spoiled food. Those concerns escalated in late May, when at least 300 detainees organized a hunger and labor strike.

Weeks after that action began, women housed in a separate unit at Delaney Hall launched a hunger strike of their own. Their demands include improvements at the facility as well as calls for ICE to release women younger than 21, women with medical conditions and mothers.

ICE maintains that detainees receive appropriate medical care.

articles.title: Tesla paid Elon Musk 2.5m times more as CEO than its average worker in 2025
articles.excerpt:
Tech billionaire’s $158.3bn deal an outlier in report showing widening gap of CEO to worker pay at top companies

Elon Musk received over 2.5m times as much compensation at Tesla as the company’s aver...
articles.body_text:
Tech billionaire’s $158.3bn deal an outlier in report showing widening gap of CEO to worker pay at top companies

Elon Musk received over 2.5m times as much compensation at Tesla as the company’s average worker, according to a new report on the growing gap between top corporate executives and their workers.

Musk’s $158.3bn pay deal was an outlier but came as the gap between CEO and worker pay continued to grow. Excluding Musk, last year the average ratio of CEO to worker pay for the top S&P 500 companies was 312 to 1, up from a 285:1 ratio in 2024. With Musk, the average pay ratio was 5,387:1, according to the executive pay watch report released this week by the AFL-CIO, the largest federation of labor unions in the US.

“In 2025, Elon Musk received the median Tesla worker’s pay every 4.23 seconds – less time than it takes to read this sentence,” states the report. “A majority of S&P 500 CEOs made more in one day than the median US worker made in one year.”

Average CEO pay, excluding Musk, was $22.8m in 2025, up from $18.9m in 2024. With Tesla accounted for, the average increases to $340.1m.

The report notes workers’ share of US national income has fallen to the lowest level since the second world war.

The report also looks at Donald Trump’s income in 2025. At $2.2bn, largely from his crypto holdings, Trump’s income rose nearly 254% from 2024. The median US worker would require 43,154 years to earn what Trump received in 2025.

“This is political grift unlike what we have ever seen in our lifetimes, perhaps ever, but it only tells part of the story of how CEOs and the Trump administration has rigged our economy to enrich themselves at the expense of working people,” said Fred Redmond, AFL-CIO’s secretary-treasurer.

“Trump’s radical budget bill that Republicans rammed through Congress last year, it made drastic cuts to healthcare, food assistance for children and families in order to give massive tax cuts for corporations and the wealthy.”

The report cited data demonstrating the economic struggles of most Americans; 33% of US adults have no retirement savings, 37% of adults do not have enough money to cover a $400 emergency expense, 26% of US adults have skipped medical care due to costs, and 23% of renters in the US have fallen behind on rent over the past year.

Tesla did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the report.

“As President Trump said, he has a lot of assets because he was a massively successful businessman prior to becoming President, which was why he was elected to office in the first place,” said a White House spokesperson in an email. “All of the President’s assets are in held in fully discretionary accounts managed by independent third-party financial institutions. There are no conflicts of interest.”

articles.title: Trump admin marks 15 straight months with zero border releases as apprehensions plunge 94%
articles.excerpt:
President Donald Trump discusses the dramatic decrease in fentanyl deaths since securing the southern border in an exclusive interview with Trace Gallagher.

President Donald Trump's administration sa...
articles.body_text:
President Donald Trump discusses the dramatic decrease in fentanyl deaths since securing the southern border in an exclusive interview with Trace Gallagher.

President Donald Trump's administration says it has gone 15 straight months without a single release at the border as of Thursday.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin's office says daily apprehensions at the border are down 94% compared to former President Joe Biden's administration and are at the lowest level seen in 30 years.

"Again this month, the results are clear: President Trump’s border security agenda is restoring order and putting the safety of the American people first," Mullin said in a statement.

"DHS remains focused on enforcing our immigration laws, securing the border, and ensuring those who enter our country illegally are removed swiftly. Thanks to the strong leadership of President Trump, we have the most secure border in history," he added.

'AMERICA FIRST' IMMIGRATION OVERHAUL BILL WOULD CODIFY TRUMP'S CAMPAIGN PROMISES ONCE AND FOR ALL

A U.S. Border Patrol agent works at the border to seal an illegal cross-border tunnel which was originally discovered on January 10, 2025, between El Paso and Ciudad Juarez, Mexico on March 11, 2025. (HERIKA MARTINEZ/AFP via Getty Images)

Meanwhile, seizures of contraband at the border in July were 26% higher than under Biden, with authorities seizing cocaine, methamphetamine, heroin, fentanyl, and marijuana.

INSIDE UNDERGROUND EL PASO STORM DRAIN SYSTEM BORDER PATROL SAYS CARTELS EXPLOIT TO SMUGGLE ILLEGAL MIGRANTS

U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) also helped enforce Trump's tariff policies, flagging $23 billion in duties identified for collection in July alone.

"Clear policy, strong enforcement, and dedicated frontline personnel are delivering results at our borders," CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott said in a statement.

U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) recruiter Gabriel Montanez helps a man fill out an application during a CBP and Border Patrol recruitment event at a public library in El Paso, Texas, U.S., September 25, 2025. REUTERS/Paul Ratje ( )

"With the support of President Trump and Secretary Mullin, CBP is securing our nation against illegal crossings, dangerous individuals, and illicit drugs while keeping lawful trade and travel moving. These results show what is possible when border security is treated as a national priority," he added.

The Trump administration is still moving to increase its immigration enforcement efforts. Last month, the House of Representatives moved toward codifying several of Trump's immigration orders.

The Permanent Trump Secure Border Act would criminalize visa overstays and increase penalties for unlawful entry, would effectively end "catch and release" policies by requiring most illegal migrants to be detained or returned while their cases are pending and tighten asylum eligibility and humanitarian parole, among other provisions.

A U.S. Department Of Homeland Security and U.S. Customs and Border Protection sign is displayed at the U.S. Customs and Border Protection Headquarters on May 18, 2025 in Washington, DC. (Kevin Carter/Getty Images)

The measure would also bolster the CBP by directing the DHS to modernize border facilities, expand staffing and workforce planning and deploy more surveillance technology, including drones, radar systems, biometric screening and DNA collection.

Fox News' Adam Pack contributed to this report.

Anders Hagstrom is a reporter with Fox News Digital covering national politics and major breaking news events.

articles.title: Alarming study finds top chatbots more likely to repeat falsehoods from the left: ‘Truly astonishing’
articles.excerpt:
Jim Agresti, president and co-founder of Just Facts, told Fox News Digital his study found leading AI chatbots spread political misinformation and frequently relied on faulty sources.

Three of the wo...
articles.body_text:
Jim Agresti, president and co-founder of Just Facts, told Fox News Digital his study found leading AI chatbots spread political misinformation and frequently relied on faulty sources.

Three of the world’s four leading artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots are more likely to fall for political falsehoods from the left than the right, while frequently backing their answers with sources that don’t support their claims or don’t exist, according to a comprehensive new study.

The study, conducted by Just Facts, tested paid versions of ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok and Claude using 100 questions on immigration, abortion, climate change, elections, crime, gun control, COVID-19 and other key issues. The questions were "designed to elicit falsehoods" from the left and the right, with each chatbot required to provide sources for its answers.

The study found ChatGPT correctly answered 94% of questions designed to elicit falsehoods from the right, compared with 75% from the left. Gemini scored 91% on the right and 76% on the left, while Claude scored 91% on the right and 81% on the left.

Grok moved in the opposite direction, scoring 73% on questions designed to elicit falsehoods from the right and 84% on those from the left, according to the study.

AI CHATBOTS TAKE HEAT OVER LEFT-WING BIAS: ‘NO LONGER BE CONSIDERED NEUTRAL’

AI apps Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini. (Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

"This study goes a lot deeper than political bias," Jim Agresti, president of the nonprofit research institute Just Facts, told Fox News Digital.

"It is meant to show how often these AIs are propagating misinformation. Now, you can be biased without being misinformed. This is a much deeper study because many studies have been done on AI political bias, and they uniformly find that they're biased to the left. But that doesn't necessarily mean they're wrong. So what I wanted to ascertain is: Are they wrong, or are they right?"

ChatGPT was the only chatbot whose difference in accuracy on questions designed to elicit falsehoods from the political left versus the political right was statistically significant at the 95% confidence level, the study found.

Notably, the study cautioned that its precisely worded questions may have given the chatbots "clear roadmaps to find the correct answers," meaning they could "perform significantly worse" on broader questions where "critical thinking is necessary to answer correctly."

"ChatGPT was effectively a C student," Agresti said. "Gemini was a C student. Claude was a B student. Grok, on the other hand, was the reverse. It was better at vetting falsehoods from the left than the right."

But Agresti said an even bigger concern was the sources the chatbots cited to support their answers.

"The thing that really jumped out at me when I started going through the sources they provided is that roughly half of the sources were illegitimate," he said.

The four chatbots cited 419 sources for their 400 answers, but many were flawed, according to the study. Among them were 104 webpages that did not exist and 77 sources that failed to answer the questions they were cited to support.

WILLIAM BENNETT, JON HAGE: AI CAN MIMIC A TEACHER, BUT IT CANNOT SHEPHERD A SOUL

The study, conducted by Just Facts and released on Tuesday, tested paid versions of ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok and Claude with questions "designed to elicit falsehoods" from the left and the right. (iStock)

Overall, the study found that just 46% of the sources cited by the chatbots were valid. ChatGPT had the highest rate at 57%, followed by Gemini at 49%, Claude at 44% and Grok at 32%.

"This was truly astonishing to me, and when I started digging deeper, I noticed that other studies had come to this conclusion as well," Agresti said.

Pointing to a 2026 study published in The Lancet and cited in the report, Agresti said that previous research found 30% to 69% of AI-generated references in biomedical contexts were "fabricated," which the report called a "well-documented failure mode" of AI models.

"The consequences of this are astonishing because we're talking about biomedicine, in other words, people's health," he said. "They're equally important in the realm of public policy because many issues have life or death implications whether we're talking about health care, crime, abortion, war and peace. The decisions people make can kill people or allow people to live."

A question designed to elicit a falsehood from the left prompted all four chatbots to say the U.S. violent crime rate was near a 50-year low in 2023. The study cited Justice Department data showing violent crime rose 37% from 2020 to 2023. By contrast, all four rejected President Donald Trump’s claim that "crime is worse than it’s ever been."

ChatGPT and Gemini also said Vice President JD Vance called school shootings a "fact of life," which the study classified as a falsehood from the left. Vance was referring to "psychos" who "want to make headlines" as a "fact of life," the study said.

In other examples classified as falsehoods from the left, all four chatbots said the Obama administration altered intelligence assessments to downplay the threat of ISIS and that men and women generally earn equal pay for equal work. The chatbots cited nonexistent or faulty sources for those answers.

CHRISTIAN UNIVERSITY AIMS TO PRODUCE 'IRREPLACEABLE' GRADUATES AS AI RESHAPES HIGHER EDUCATION

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman speaks during the 2026 Infrastructure Summit in Washington, D.C., on March 11, 2026. (Kylie Cooper/Reuters)

On the other side, Grok incorrectly said all illegal immigrants have committed a crime "by virtue of their presence" in the U.S., while all four chatbots correctly said the Earth’s lower-atmosphere temperature has risen about 1.1 degrees Fahrenheit since the 1980s, according to the study.

Agresti warned users against treating AI chatbots as experts, referring to OpenAI CEO Sam Altman’s description of GPT-5 last year as being like having a "team of Ph.D.-level experts in your pocket."

"What my study definitively showed is it's more like having a B student in your pocket, because that's how well they scored on these tests," he said.

Agresti also highlighted AI sycophancy, the tendency of chatbots to validate users and "feed into" their biases, calling it a "recipe for disaster." To minimize the influence, the study used a freshly installed browser and new accounts to prevent prior interactions from influencing its results.

"If you have a certain political bias, AIs are going to feed into that, and they're going to state it with very strident confidence that will make you believe you're right," he said.

Still, Agresti acknowledged he doesn’t "have enough knowledge" to explain what’s happening inside the models to produce the results.

"That's a question for programmers and the people who make them, and I would hope that they would answer them and fix these models and make them better because they are powerful, they can read at the speed of light, but they are incredibly sloppy, dishonest, politically misinformed, and this is a danger," he said.

Agresti said the takeaway isn’t to abandon AI, but to "never blindly trust the results" and ensure its sources exist and support its claims.

"When Ronald Reagan was negotiating nuclear disarmament with the Soviet Union, he famously said, 'Trust but verify,'" Agresti said. "I think the take-home from this study is even stronger, and it's this: Don't trust, verify."

Other research on AI political bias has painted a different picture in the past. Fox News Digital previously reported that Dartmouth College's Polarization Research Lab ranked Gemini as the least political in 2025, while an early 2025 Manhattan Institute report found Grok a close second to Gemini in terms of political bias.

"Gemini is designed to provide neutral, accurate responses that do not favor any political viewpoint, and we rigorously test our models to ensure they stay that way," a Google spokesperson said in a statement to Fox News Digital, adding that they were unable to replicate all of the responses in the study.

An Anthropic spokesperson pushed back on the study’s methodology, telling Fox News Digital in a statement its multiple-choice format does not reflect typical Claude conversations and highlighting the company’s efforts to ensure political neutrality through training, testing and evaluations.

"We train Claude to treat different political viewpoints equally and test extensively for bias before every model launch," the spokesperson said. "We've open-sourced those evaluations so anyone can check our work, and welcome independent testing of our models. We understand that this study limited each model to multiple-choice answers on 100 questions, which doesn't reflect how people normally use Claude, particularly on political topics. In a real conversation, Claude is designed to respond at a natural length, with room for important context and multiple perspectives."

An OpenAI spokesperson told Fox News Digital that ChatGPT "is designed to be objective by default," adding that its tools "surface relevant information from a range of sources, and clearly show those sources so that you can explore and assess the reliability of the information directly yourself."

"We continually measure our political bias evaluations and disclose our findings," the spokesperson said in a statement.

Fox News Digital reached out to xAI for comment but did not receive a response.

Kiera McDonald is a Production Assistant for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Florida father gunned down while intervening in fight after dropping daughter off for first day of school
articles.excerpt: The Orange County Sheriff's Department said Vazquez, 26, fatally shot 56-year-old Daryl Alexander Hill on Tuesday after Hill intervened in a roadside argument between Vazquez and a woman. (Credit: Ora...
articles.body_text:
The Orange County Sheriff's Department said Vazquez, 26, fatally shot 56-year-old Daryl Alexander Hill on Tuesday after Hill intervened in a roadside argument between Vazquez and a woman. (Credit: Orange County Sheriff's Department)

A Florida father who had just dropped off his daughter for her first day of elementary school was shot and killed after trying to intervene in a fight between a man and a woman, police and reports said.

Daryl Hill, 56, now leaves behind his wife, two adult children and his 10-year-old daughter following the incident Tuesday morning near Wolf Lake Elementary School in Apopka, according to FOX 35 Orlando.

"He’s got the biggest heart in the entire world," Damon Hill, his son, told the station. "He loved everybody... He just loved his fellow person, and he was very non-judgmental."

The Orange County Sheriff’s Office said the shooting unfolded after witnesses described seeing a man and woman fighting inside a vehicle, before the vehicle crashed and the brawl spilled outside.

BYSTANDER SHOT DEAD AFTER INTERVENING IN FLORIDA MAN, WOMAN'S ROADSIDE FIGHT; MURDER SUSPECT WAS OUT ON BOND

Daryl Hill, center, leaves behind his wife, two adult children and 10-year-old daughter, according to FOX 35 Orlando. (Damon Hill/WOFL)

"Witnessing that altercation, a Good Samaritan attempted to intervene and was shot. That man, 56-year-old Daryl Alexander Hill, later died at the hospital," the sheriff's office said.

"Mr. Hill was simply trying to help someone who appeared to be in distress when he was shot by 26-year-old Raul Lionel Vazquez. Vazquez was arrested on a charge of Second-Degree Murder," it added.

Suzanne Hill, Daryl’s wife, told Spectrum News 13 that her husband was a "friend, family and stranger: he cared for everybody and helped everybody and always stepped in, which I think is ultimately what took his life."

Police said the shooting happened at Plymouth Sorrento and West Ponkan roads in Apopka, which is down the road from the elementary school.

Before Hill was shot, Vazquez and a woman, Kaidy Honaker, were seen by multiple witnesses fighting inside their white Chevy Silverado pickup truck when it crashed into a black Lexus, according to an arrest affidavit obtained by Fox News Digital. The two continued their heated altercation on the sidewalk.

VIDEO SHOWS MOMENTS BEFORE ARMY VETERAN WAS FATALLY SHOT IN WALMART PARKING LOT DISPUTE

Daryl Hill, left, allegedly was shot and killed by suspect Raul Lionel Vazquez on Tuesday, Aug. 11, 2026, in Apopka, Fla. (Camil Reyes/WOFL; Orange County Sheriff's Office)

Vazquez, who was seen shirtless and wearing no shoes, got in Honaker's face and appeared to be yelling and pointing at her, the affidavit said.

Two witnesses said they saw Hill riding a bicycle nearby and told authorities that he got involved in the argument, which led to Vazquez and Hill tackling each other into the bushes, per the affidavit.

According to the affidavit, Honaker joined the fight as well, later saying she did so to pull Hill off Vazquez.

An undated photo of Daryl Alexander Hill and his wife, Suzy Hill. Hill leaves behind a 10-year-old daughter. (GoFundMe)

After the fight in the bushes, Hill began running away from Vazquez and Honaker, yelling "help" with his hands in the air, the affidavit said.

Vazquez retrieved what was later determined to be a shotgun from his pickup truck and fired one round, hitting Hill and causing him to fall to the ground, according to the affidavit.

In an interview with investigators, Vazquez offered "many different accounts" of what happened but said that Hill "was fighting him and getting the better of him," according to the affidavit.

At the time of the shooting, Vazquez was out on bond for aggravated assault with a deadly weapon.

FOX 35 reported that a judge has since revoked that bond and ordered him held without bond in that case and for the second-degree murder charge.

Greg Norman is a reporter at Fox News Digital.
