Laura Ingraham, Sean Hannity and Greg Gutfeld bring Fox News viewers their fresh takes on the top news of the day.

President Donald Trump said that he is nominating federal judge Lee Rudofsky to serv...
articles.body_text:
Laura Ingraham, Sean Hannity and Greg Gutfeld bring Fox News viewers their fresh takes on the top news of the day.

President Donald Trump said that he is nominating federal judge Lee Rudofsky to serve on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit.

"I am pleased to announce the nomination of Lee Rudofsky to the United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit!" Trump exclaimed in a Wednesday Truth Social post.

Rudofsky is currently serving on the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Arkansas, a position to which Trump nominated him back in 2019.

FEDERAL APPEALS COURT CLEARS WAY FOR DESANTIS-BACKED LAW RESTRICTING CHILDREN AT SOME DRAG SHOWS

U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Arkansas Judge Lee Rudofsky speaks during the Federalist Society's National Lawyers Convention in Washington, D.C., Nov. 7, 2025. (REUTERS/Nathan Howard)

"Lee is currently a distinguished Federal District Court Judge in Arkansas. He previously was Solicitor General of Arkansas, and Assistant General Counsel of Walmart. He is a Graduate of Harvard Law School and Cornell University. Lee will be a rock solid defender of the Constitution on the Eighth Circuit. Congratulations Lee!" the president added in his post.

Arkansas Lt. Gov. Leslie Rutledge and state Attorney General Tim Griffin both congratulated Rudofsky.

FEDERAL JUDGE BLOCKS TRUMP ADMINISTRATION FROM RESTRICTING MAIL-IN BALLOTS AHEAD OF MIDTERMS

U.S. President Donald Trump boards Air Force One on Aug. 9, 2026 at Morristown Airport in Morristown, N.J. (Eric Lee/Getty Images)

"I am proud to congratulate Judge Lee Rudofsky on his nomination to the United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit. When I appointed Judge Rudofsky to serve as Arkansas’s first Solicitor General, I had long recognized his legal acumen and knew he would serve Arkansas with distinction. On the federal district court, Judge Rudofsky has adhered to the original text of our constitution and applied the rule of law fairly and impartially. I am confident he will continue to apply the law faithfully," Rutledge, who previously served as the state's attorney general, declared in a post on X.

"Judge Rudofsky is a once-in-a-generation jurist, and I ask the United States Senate to swiftly confirm President Trump’s nomination," she added.

TRUMP'S WHITE HOUSE BALLROOM FOES FACE 'VERY TOUGH ARGUMENT' AT SUPREME COURT, LEGAL EXPERTS SAY

Lee Philip Rudofsky testifies during a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on his nomination for U.S. district judge for the Eastern District of Arkansas along with other judicial nominees on Wednesday July 31, 2019. (Caroline Brehman/CQ Roll Call)

"Congratulations to Judge Lee Rudofsky on his nomination by @realDonaldTrump to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit. Judge Rudofsky’s devotion to the rule of law, his fidelity to the Constitution & his unrivaled intellect & legal acumen make him an exceptional choice!" Griffin wrote on X.

Alex Nitzberg is a writer for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: ‘Lauf’ and ‘minceur’: the words that made a 13-year-old from Melbourne a world Scrabble champion
articles.excerpt:
Dineth Fernando – who moved to Australia with his family in February – says he just needed to ‘find the word and play – that’s all’

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Dineth...
articles.body_text:
Dineth Fernando – who moved to Australia with his family in February – says he just needed to ‘find the word and play – that’s all’

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Dineth Fernando’s first language isn’t English and he only arrived in Melbourne six months ago – but already he’s claimed an international Scrabble title with an Australian flag draped around his shoulders.

The 13-year-old won the 2026 world youth Scrabble championships in the Kenyan capital of Nairobi over the weekend, becoming the third Australian representative in the competition’s history to take out the prize.

During the three-day tournament, Dineth played 24 games of the classic word game, going head-to-head against more than 130 opponents from 15 different countries.

“It took a lot of stress and effort to navigate through the days,” Dineth, who moved with his family in February from Sri Lanka, said.

“But I just needed to concentrate on the game, nothing else.

“Like, don’t care if there is a live camera going on, I just needed to jumble the rack, find the word and play – that’s all.”

This was Dineth’s third attempt at the world championships, and the trip to Nairobi had already forced him to contend with jetlag on top of the nerves.

But after more than 20 hours of play, and carefully placed words including “lauf” (a run in bobsleighing), “novelese” (a style of writing characteristic of poor novels), “minceur” (a French word for thinness), “histrio” (an archaic word meaning actor) and “postering”, the 13-year-old emerged victorious on Sunday.

Prasanna Fernando almost cried when his son was crowned the world youth Scrabble champion.

“I sometimes still can’t believe he actually won it because the level of competition was extremely high.

“But I always knew he was capable of doing it one day.”

Dineth got his first taste for the game when he and his family were still living in Sri Lanka.

At eight years old, he joined the school Scrabble club before hiring a private coach as he flew all over the country to compete.

His family moved to Australia in February for his father’s work, but he continued his pursuit for Scrabble greatness, entering competitions and playing against people like Melbourne-based two-time Scrabble world champion and 2006 youth Scrabble winner David Eldar, and even beating world champion finalist Harshan Lamabadusuriya.

His accolades quickly grew, becoming runner-up at the Wodonga open Scrabble championship, winning the Ballarat open championship and eventually taking out the Australian youth prize.

Scrabble Victoria secretary, Carol Johnsen, has faced the teenager a few times, and though he had luck on his side, she says he is also a force to be reckoned with.

“The tiles just flowed for him: he got the X and the Z and the Q and they all went in the right places.

“I had no hope, and he’s beat me by over 200 points each time.”

Dineth spends more than three hours a day studying Scrabble words and believes his discipline and hard work gave him an edge at the youth competition.

Though English is not his first language, he does not see this as an issue, since the game’s dictionary is a combination of many languages including English, Latin, French and more.

Nigel Richards, a five-time world champion became famous for winning Scrabble tournaments in languages he didn’t speak, taking out the French title in 2015 and 2018, and the Spanish-language competition in 2024.

For those at the top levels of Scrabble, it is closer to mathematics and pattern recognition than a language game, according to Johnsen.

But Dineth’s favourite thing about Scrabble is the opportunity it offers for him to learn new words.

After an almost 12,000km trip home, the 13-year-old returned to school on Thursday, where a hero’s welcome was waiting.

“It was a really great feeling that everyone – my friends and teachers – wished me,” he said.

He’s now got his eyes on the 2027 competition and is hoping to become the first youth champion to defend their title.

articles.title: UK defends seizing shadow fleet tanker after Putin threat
articles.excerpt:
Royal Marine Commandos were involved in the operation to seize the MT Smyrtos

The UK government has defended its seizure of a Russian "shadow fleet" oil tanker in the English Channel, after Russian P...
articles.body_text:
Royal Marine Commandos were involved in the operation to seize the MT Smyrtos

The UK government has defended its seizure of a Russian "shadow fleet" oil tanker in the English Channel, after Russian President Vladimir Putin threatened to "respond in kind".

The Smyrtos was taken to be anchored off Weymouth after Royal Marines Commandos intercepted and boarded it in a first-of-its-kind operation to disrupt the sanctioned tanker in June.

The vessel's captain, Ajay Pant, has been charged with breaching Russian sanctions, accused of directly or indirectly supplying or delivering prohibited Russian oil.

Overseeing Russian navy drills in the Pacific Ocean, Putin scolded Western countries for "seizing our vessels", branding such action "nothing other than piracy and banditry".

"If these plans are put into practice, we will have to respond in kind," Putin warned on Wednesday.

"And not necessarily in the waters where raids on our ships and vessels are planned, but wherever we deem it necessary and appropriate, anywhere."

Viktor Liina, commander of Russia's Pacific Fleet, accused Western countries such as Britain and France of operating their own "shadow fleets".

"We have the capacity to inspect and detain vessels of unfriendly states and their shadow fleets, and interagency cooperation is in place, ready to begin addressing these challenges," Liina said.

In response to Putin's comments, the UK government said Britain's armed forces and law-enforcement officers had boarded the Smyrtos "in full accordance with international law".

"The UK is disrupting and deterring shadow fleet vessels and their harmful maritime activity which is fuelling Russia's war with Ukraine," a government spokesperson said.

The spokesperson said unlike Russia's shadow fleet, "UK armed forces and commercial vessels operate firmly in line with international maritime law".

Watch: MoD footage shows commandos boarding and searching the tanker

Western nations allege Russia has been operating a "shadow fleet" to evade international sanctions imposed on its oil exports.

The UK Ministry of Defence says Russia has a fleet of more than 700 vessels, responsible for carrying 75% of the country's sanctioned oil.

This oil is a "critical lifeline for the Kremlin" in "sustaining Russia's illegal war", the MoD says.

Putin's comments come as the European Union intensifies pressure on Russia's shadow fleet.

In his remarks to Russian sailors, Putin singled out the EU, accusing member states of violating international maritime law and "attempting to restrict the movement of vessels belonging to our economic operators".

Many Western countries imposed sanctions on Russian energy following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Moscow has been accused of dodging them by shipping oil on aged tankers often with obscure ownership or insurance.

To combat this tactic, in 2024 the EU began sanctioning individual shadow fleet vessels – "Putin's dark fleet", as the European Council, the bloc's top group of national leaders, put it.

More than 630 vessels are sanctioned as of mid-August 2026, meaning they are banned from EU ports.

Meanwhile, several individual European countries have been seizing or detaining Russian-linked vessels or have carried out boardings or detentions when sanctions violations are suspected.

Most recently, the Italian navy, in conjunction with other EU countries, boarded a tanker in the central Mediterranean suspected of not being entitled to fly the flag it claimed.

Although that inspection did not result in a seizure of the vessel, others have.

Since the start of the year, nine shadow fleet tankers suspected of circumventing sanctions have been seized around the EU.

Royal Marines board Russian shadow fleet oil tanker in English Channel

What happened to Russian 'shadow fleet' tanker crew?

articles.title: South Korean airport becomes busiest in world for global traffic amid Iran war
articles.excerpt:
Incheon airport had 38.39m international passengers in first half of 2026, as traffic diverted from Middle East hubs

South Korea’s Incheon airport has become the world’s busiest airport for internati...
articles.body_text:
Incheon airport had 38.39m international passengers in first half of 2026, as traffic diverted from Middle East hubs

South Korea’s Incheon airport has become the world’s busiest airport for international passengers, in part owing to disruption in the Middle East caused by the Iran war.

The airport, South Korea’s main gateway, about 30 miles (48km) west of Seoul, handled 38.39 million international passengers in the first half of 2026, according to preliminary figures compiled by the Airports Council International (ACI), the global trade body for airports.

Heathrow in the UK was second, with 37.79 million, followed by Changi airport in Singapore with 34.53 million.

It is the first time Incheon has topped the international passenger rankings since opening in 2001. The airport was 10th in the world in 2002, rising to fifth in 2018 and third in 2024 and 2025.

Part of the increase was attributed to disruption caused by the US-Iran conflict, which weakened the role of Middle Eastern hubs such as Dubai and diverted some transfer traffic to alternative routes through east Asia, Incheon International Airport Corporation (IIAC) was quoted as saying by the Yonhap news agency.

Incheon’s international passenger traffic was up 6.3% year on year overall, with rising numbers of foreign visitors also contributing to the increase.

Foreigners accounted for 39.3% of Incheon’s passengers in the first half of the year, up from 35.2% for the whole of 2025. The proportion reached a record 44.4% in the second quarter, with IIAC attributing the increase largely to growing numbers of visitors from China and Japan, according to local media.

Heathrow, in west London, recorded 40 million passengers in total in the first half of the year, including both domestic and international travellers, its busiest first half on record. Passenger traffic to Asia-Pacific rose 7.9%, while capacity to the Middle East reportedly fell 16.5% owing to the regional conflict.

Earlier this week Istanbul overtook Heathrow as Europe’s busiest airport by total passenger numbers. Figures published on Tuesday showed 7.9 million passengers passed through Heathrow’s terminals in July, compared with Istanbul’s 8.15 million.

Incheon has also expanded its role as an international hub. It serves 101 airlines flying to 183 cities, including 158 international passenger destinations.

A four-phase expansion completed in late 2024 increased the airport’s annual capacity to 106 million passengers.

Kim Beom-ho, the acting president of IIAC, said the ranking reflected “the support of the government, the public’s encouragement and the hard work of everyone stationed at the airport”.

South Korea also lays claim to the world’s busiest air route. The domestic corridor between Gimpo airport and Jeju island had 14.4 million seats scheduled in 2025, according to the aviation data provider OAG, more than any other route in the world.

articles.title: FIFA’s Infantino backed by six Arab federations including Qatar and Morocco
articles.excerpt: Six ‌heads of Arab national football associations, including 2022 World Cup host Qatar and 2030 World ⁠Cup cohost Morocco, have joined the growing ⁠backing for FIFA President Gianni Infantino with foo...
articles.body_text:
Six ‌heads of Arab national football associations, including 2022 World Cup host Qatar and 2030 World ⁠Cup cohost Morocco, have joined the growing ⁠backing for FIFA President Gianni Infantino with football’s world governing body in crisis after a failed private investment plan.

Infantino, who ⁠is seeking re-election next year, has faced open revolt after three confederations – UEFA, AFC and CONCACAF – called for him to quit over his aborted ⁠bid to bring private investment into FIFA competitions, including the World Cup.

The Swiss administrator had proposed carving off the commercial rights to the World Cup and selling 20 percent to private investors to raise about $4.2bn.

“Recognising the important role of ‌Arab football in bringing people together and strengthening cooperation among football associations across the Arab world, we … express our full support for Mr Gianni Infantino, president of FIFA, and reaffirm our confidence in his leadership and continued commitment to the development of football worldwide,” the heads of the six federations said in a joint statement.

The statement was signed by ⁠the heads of the national federations of Qatar, ⁠Lebanon, Morocco, Sudan, Egypt and Mauritania. Four of the six signatories are also FIFA Council members.

“We deeply appreciate Mr Infantino’s sustained efforts to advance football globally, expand opportunities across all regions ⁠and strengthen the game’s role in bringing people and communities together,” they said.

“We look forward to continuing our ⁠close cooperation with him towards a stronger and ⁠more prosperous future for world football, expanding opportunities and further enhancing Arab football’s contribution to the global game.”

Infantino’s withdrawn proposal came with a $20m grant for member associations for the next ‌funding cycle, an amount that could have been doubled if they had signed the deal.

Despite the opposition of the three confederations in Europe, Asia, North and Central America and the Caribbean, which represent 136 of the ‌211 ‌member associations who will vote in the FIFA presidential election in March, Infantino still has plenty of allies in the game.

articles.title: Harvard-China links unearthed as Congress finds 140 papers co-authored by CCP military universities
articles.excerpt: Rep. Pat Fallon unveiled legislation that would strip federal intelligence-related funding from colleges maintaining ties to Chinese Communist Party-linked groups, arguing it is necessary to protect s...
articles.body_text:
Rep. Pat Fallon unveiled legislation that would strip federal intelligence-related funding from colleges maintaining ties to Chinese Communist Party-linked groups, arguing it is necessary to protect sensitive U.S. research and national security.

FIRST ON FOX: Harvard allegedly failed to adequately safeguard research collaborations with Chinese institutions, including universities tied to Beijing’s military and defense-industrial base, according to a report from the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party.

Researchers affiliated with the New England Ivy League co-authored more than 140 publications with other researchers affiliated with a group of Chinese universities, according to the report reviewed by Fox News Digital ahead of its public release.

The "Seven Sons of National Defense" are a group of Chinese universities identified by the Pentagon and other U.S. officials as central to China’s defense research and military modernization efforts. The House Committee created to crackdown on China argues Harvard’s approach to research security opened the door for collaborations that could advance technological and military capabilities of the hostile nation.

Harvard also reported received more than $600 million from China under the federal Section 117 foreign-gift disclosure system — more than any other American university, according to the Education Department dashboard cited in the report. The committee argues the U.S. university's financial ties to China heighten the need for strict oversight of its research partnerships and foreign-funding disclosures.

Banners hanging from Memorial Church on the Harvard University campus in Cambridge, Massachusetts, US, on Tuesday, May 27, 2025. (Sophie Park/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

HARVARD TOPS NATION IN FOREIGN CASH HAUL AS COTTON DEMANDS PROBE INTO CHINA FUNDING

The stakes in the latest report extend far beyond Harvard. U.S. officials have warned for years that China uses academic partnerships and access to Western research to advance CCP strategic capabilities in military, surveillance and other areas.

The House Select Committee on China argues that universities receiving U.S. taxpayer funding must do more than meet the narrowest legal requirements when collaborating with institutions embedded in China’s military research system, particularly when it comes to technology with potential defense or military uses.

The report highlights a 2023 paper on bio-inspired soft robots for deep-sea exploration co-authored by a Harvard-affiliated researcher and a researcher from Beihang University, one of the Seven Sons institutions. Beihang, also known as Beijing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics, has appeared on the Commerce Department’s Entity List since 2001.

The committee report argues the work examined in the paper has potential military applications, including underwater detection, while Harvard’s research-compliance office characterized the project as nonmilitary research.

FOREIGN ROBOT BAN TARGETS CHINA OVER SECURITY FEARS

Harvard researchers also co-authored a 2023 paper with a researcher at China’s National University of Defense Technology, another institution on a U.S. restricted list, according to the report. That study involved magnetic materials and acknowledged partial support from the U.S. Army Research Office.

An image from a 2023 paper on bioinspired soft robots for deep-sea exploration co-authored by researchers affiliated with Harvard and China’s Beihang University. (House Select Committee on the CCP)

The committee said it reviewed publications spanning dozens of disciplines and found that engineering accounted for the largest share of Harvard-affiliated research involving Seven Sons institutions.

"From allowing violence against anti-China protestors to collaborating with entities linked to the PLA, Harvard has made serious mistakes and must act now to prevent more. It should use this investigation as a catalyst for significant reforms that end CCP influence on campus and prioritize secure American research," committee chairman Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., said in a statement.

The report also examines Harvard’s executive education program with China’s National Healthcare Security Administration, which trained Chinese health officials on international health-insurance systems.

According to the report, attendance and registration records show officials affiliated with the Xinjiang Production and Construction Corps, or XPCC, were listed in connection with some sessions. The Treasury Department sanctioned XPCC in 2020 over human-rights abuses against Uyghurs and other ethnic minorities in Xinjiang.

The report acknowledges it is unclear whether XPCC officials ultimately attended every program in question.

It alleges, however, that Harvard had advance participant information for a 2020 online session that included XPCC-affiliated officials and did not take further action.

Harvard professor Winnie Yip, who helped organize the executive education program, told committee investigators she did not know XPCC was a sanctioned entity at the time and had not received training on sanctions compliance, according to the report.

The report further alleges Harvard’s research-security practices focused too narrowly on technical legal compliance and failed to account for broader national-security risks posed by work with Chinese military-linked institutions.

It cites testimony from Harvard research official John H. Shaw, who said the university evaluates research collaborations case by case and does not prohibit all work involving robotics or Chinese institutions. The committee criticized that approach, arguing research with entities embedded in China’s military-civil fusion system can have military applications even when the research is unclassified and intended for publication.

Chinese President Xi Jinping, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, reviews the troops during his inspection of the Chinese People's Liberation Army PLA garrison stationed in the Macao Special Administrative Region, south China, Dec. 20, 2024. (Li Gang/Xinhua via Getty Images)

The report also raises questions about Harvard Global Research and Support Services, a nonprofit affiliated with the university that can accept awards when Harvard is unable to accept a sponsor’s terms directly. The committee alleges the entity could be used to circumvent federal foreign-gift reporting requirements, an allegation Harvard will likely dispute.

Harvard did not respond to Fox News’ request for comment on the House Committee report’s findings.

The report recommends that Harvard prohibit research relationships with entities on U.S. government restricted or sanctioned lists and centralize its research-security oversight. It also urges Congress to strengthen foreign-funding disclosure requirements for universities.

articles.title: MORNING GLORY: Democrat El-Sayed reminds us just one senator can do great damage to our military
articles.excerpt:
Fox News contributor Hugh Hewitt discusses far-left streamer Hasan Piker campaigning for Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed on ‘One Nation.’

It is not often that I write criticall...
articles.body_text:
Fox News contributor Hugh Hewitt discusses far-left streamer Hasan Piker campaigning for Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed on ‘One Nation.’

It is not often that I write critically of a Republican United States senator. But that happened in February 2023, when Alabama Sen. Tommy Tuberville placed a hold on military promotions to protest a Department of Defense policy that covered travel expenses for service members seeking reproductive healthcare across state lines. Tuberville's hold ultimately delayed the promotions of more than 400 senior military officers, many of whom were colonels or Navy captains awaiting promotion to general or flag rank, for roughly 10 months.

The "Tuberville Blockade" upended the lives and careers of hundreds of Army, Air Force and Marine Corps colonels and Navy captains by seriously disrupting carefully planned career paths and assignments. It also disrupted the carefully constructed career paths of the generals and admirals who were sidelined by the ill-considered embargo.

Career military officers ought never again to be held hostage for political goals. Sen. Tuberville eventually relented after months of mounting pressure from senators in both parties. He lifted his blanket "hold" after long meetings with his Senate colleagues, who emphasized to him that he was damaging the careers of people who had provided exemplary service over decades.

MORNING GLORY: MICHIGAN’S DEMOCRATIC SENATE PRIMARY HAD TWO WINNERS — BUT ONLY ONE WAS ON THE BALLOT

Sen. Tuberville is almost certainly going to be the next governor of Alabama, and hopefully he will be a better governor for having learned from his mistake. But the precedent he set in 2023 should alert everyone to why a radical leftist like Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed ought never to hold the office of United States senator.

U.S. Sen. Tommy Tuberville, R-Ala., speaks to reporters as he returns to his office at the U.S. Capitol on Feb. 10, 2026 in Washington, D.C. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

El-Sayed is a sworn enemy of the State of Israel, and I fear that it is very unlikely that he will be a supporter of the American military. El-Sayed has also repeatedly appeared with controversial left-wing streamer Hasan Piker, including at campaign rallies. His staunch allegiance to Piker telegraphs exactly what he could do if he beats Republican Mike Rogers in the fall: wreak havoc on our military and Israel’s defenses. El-Sayed has already called for a complete embargo on weapons sales to Israel — even defensive weapons.

El-Sayed supports "the immediate and comprehensive enforcement of U.S. laws that condition the provision of military aid and sales." He argues this means "an immediate arms embargo on Israel," and El-Sayed specifically rejects the distinction between offensive and defensive weapons, meaning his position includes weapons such as Iron Dome interceptors, not merely offensive bombs and missiles.

This stance places him among the most outspoken Senate candidates opposing U.S. military support for Israel. As a true hater of Israel, would El-Sayed dust off the Tuberville playbook to try to bring aid to Israel to an end? There is no reason voters should assume he would hesitate to do so.  There’s a precedent, and it is easy to hear a Sen. El-Sayed arguing that he is just deploying the same tactic that a Republican senator used.

ABDUL EL-SAYED SAYS RALLYING WITH HASAN PIKER DOESN'T MEAN HE ENDORSES 'AMERICA DESERVED 9/11' REMARK

The question for Michigan voters is not whether one senator could single-handedly shut off every American weapon or dollar flowing to Israel. He could not. But Senator Tuberville’s 2023 blockade demonstrated how much disruption a determined senator can cause by exploiting the Senate’s rules and customary procedures to delay action and force political confrontations.

It is difficult to imagine El-Sayed losing sleep over the damage he would impose on the U.S. military. That’s the possibility Michigan voters have to consider when they cast ballots this fall.

President Donald Trump, center, and GOP Senate candidate former Rep. Mike Rogers, left, listen as Rep. John James, a Republican gubernatorial candidate, speaks at an event at the General Motors Proving Ground Monday, July 27, 2026, in Milford, Mich. (Paul Sancya/AP Photo)

There are a few pro-defense Democrats left, including Michigan’s own Elissa Slotkin. But just as GOP senators would not publicly criticize their colleague in 2023, the handful of Democrats who are serious about national security would likely adhere to the unwritten code of the Senate that prohibits public attacks on colleagues from their own party conference.

So the Michigan Senate race is the most important election in the country this year. The Republican volunteers willing to go to the battleground state and campaign for Rogers will be participating in a cause much bigger than themselves.

They will be protecting the country’s national security. El-Sayed isn’t simply an extremist. He’s a dangerous radical who should not be in a position to harm the country’s armed forces.

Hugh Hewitt is a Fox News contributor and host of "The Hugh Hewitt Show" heard weekday afternoons from 3 PM to 6 PM ET on the Salem Radio Network, and simulcast on Salem News Channel. Hugh drives Americans home on the East Coast and to lunch on the West Coast on over 400 affiliates nationwide, and on all the streaming platforms where SNC can be seen. He is a frequent guest on the Fox News Channel’s news roundtable, hosted by Bret Baier weekdays at 6pm ET. A son of Ohio and a graduate of Harvard College and the University of Michigan Law School, Hewitt has been a Professor of Law at Chapman University’s Fowler School of Law since 1996 where he teaches Constitutional Law. Hewitt launched his eponymous radio show from Los Angeles in 1990. Hewitt has frequently appeared on every major national news television network, hosted television shows for PBS and MSNBC, written for every major American paper, has authored a dozen books and moderated a score of Republican candidate debates, most recently the November 2023 Republican presidential debate in Miami and four Republican presidential debates in the 2015-16 cycle. Hewitt focuses his radio show and his column on the Constitution, national security, American politics and the Cleveland Browns and Guardians. Hewitt has interviewed tens of thousands of guests from Democrats Hillary Clinton and John Kerry to Republican Presidents George W. Bush and Donald Trump over his 40 years in broadcasting. This column previews the lead story that will drive his radio/ TV show today.

articles.title: Polls open in Clacton, where Farage spent more than £10,000 in byelection against Count Binface – UK politics live
articles.excerpt:
The Reform UK leader resigned as the MP for Clacton at the start of July and forced a byelection

Good morning. In the media, August is known as the “silly season”. With parliament not sitting and man...
articles.body_text:
The Reform UK leader resigned as the MP for Clacton at the start of July and forced a byelection

Good morning. In the media, August is known as the “silly season”. With parliament not sitting and many people on holiday, there is less proper news than normal, which means the nonsense stories get (even) more attention than usual. We are almost slap bang in the middle of the month, and today we’ve got a silly season classic in Clacton, where Nigel Farage, the Reform UK candidate, is fighting a byelection in which his main opponent is a joke candidate who dresses up as a dustbin.

Farage is not inherently silly. Few politicians have been more consequential over the past quarter of a century (because he did more than any other single individual to make the Brexit referendum happen); for most of the past 16 months his party has had a big poll lead and he has a very realistic chance of being the next PM; and even if he doesn’t become PM, his hard-right, anti-migrant, crass, crypto-friendly populism will have changed British politics significantly.

But this byelection is rather absurd because it is essentially pointless; all it will do is postpone, not resolve, the verdict on the financial sleaze allegations that Farage is facing (his alleged failure to properly declare donations, including a £5m gift from a cryptocurrency billionaire).

Voting started in Clacton about two hours ago.

Normally there is not much new to report on polling day. But Politico has published a good story by John Johnston and he reveals that Reform UK has spent more than £10,000 during the election campaign on social media adverts designed to help it see off the threat from Count Binface. Johnston says:

double quotation markPOLITICO analysis of the Reform UK leader’s digital campaign messages shows that Farage has run a twin-track strategy in the seaside seat as polls open Thursday. The two key themes of the digital air war have been painting Farage as a champion for local residents — as well as an insurgent leader harried by the “establishment” machine.

Farage and his party have spent more than £10,000 pushing those messages via ads on Meta’s platforms — which include Facebook and Instagram — in the campaign so far.

Johnston says Farage is the only candidate in the byelection using “paid Meta features to bolster his online campaign”. He says:

double quotation markAlmost £1,000 has been spent on videos of Farage urging local supporters to request the party deliver and install an “I’m with Nigel” garden sign. Meanwhile, around £500 went to ads asking voters to return their postal votes and “send a message to the establishment.”

The largest single sum — between £4,000-£4,500 — was spent on an almost five-minute campaign video in which Farage waxes lyrical about the connection he’s made with local constituents, while claiming his party’s surging success has resulted in the powers-that-be using “foul means” to hamper him.

“Rather than being judged by the political class and the mainstream media, I am going to let you, the voters in the Clacton constituency, make a decision,” he said. “I want you to be my judge, not the political elite.”

There is not much else happening in Westminster politics. But it is a big day for A-level students, with results out this morning. Tom Ambrose is covering that on a separate live blog.

You can use this to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints. There is a longer post here about how we hope this will work.

articles.title: New Mississippi law expands death penalty to include inmates on child sexual battery convictions
articles.excerpt:
James Duckett was recently executed for the 1987 rape and murder of 11-year-old Tereasa McAbee. Investigators believe he also Jeanifer Weldon that same year. (Credit: WTVT)

A new Mississippi law adde...
articles.body_text:
James Duckett was recently executed for the 1987 rape and murder of 11-year-old Tereasa McAbee. Investigators believe he also Jeanifer Weldon that same year. (Credit: WTVT)

A new Mississippi law added sexual battery of a child under 12 to the list of crimes eligible for the death penalty.

Senate Bill 2821, which took effect July 1, creates the crime of "capital sexual battery" and allows prosecutors to seek the death penalty against defendants 18 or older in qualifying cases involving victims younger than 12.

If a defendant is convicted, the jury must unanimously find at least two specific aggravating factors beyond a reasonable doubt before the defendant is eligible for the death penalty. At least 8 of the 12 jurors must then recommend death. But if the death penalty is not recommended by jurors, the mandatory sentence would be life in prison without parole.

ACCUSED CHARLIE KIRK ASSASSIN TYLER ROBINSON ASKS JUDGE TO TAKE POTENTIAL DEATH PENALTY OFF TABLE

A new Mississippi law added sexual battery of a child under 12 to the list of crimes eligible for the death penalty.

State Sen. Jeremy England, the bill's author, said the legislation seeks to give the worst punishment for crimes against the state's most vulnerable population.

"That is a crime that, I think, shocks the conscience, certainly. Those are the worst types of crimes against the most innocent of our citizens here in Mississippi," England said, according to WLBT.

But critics question whether capital punishment serves as a deterrent to crimes against young victims or if it could lead to children becoming too afraid to come forward knowing that doing so may end someone's life.

The law marks a shift from previous state policy restricting capital punishment to inmates convicted on murder charges. (The Promise of Justice Initiative via AP)

Abraham Bonowitz, executive director of Death Penalty Action, told the outlet he once supported the death penalty but changed his position, arguing that executions are unnecessary when a life sentence keeps an inmate permanently behind bars.

"There is no need for executions when we can throw away the key," Bonowitz said.

TWO FLORIDA INMATES DIE IN RARE DOUBLE EXECUTION AFTER SCOTUS DENIES STAYS

Senate Bill 2821 took effect on July 1. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)

Bonowitz also said extending the death penalty to child sexual assault cases could deter victims from alerting authorities of the abuse they endured.

"Most of those kinds of crimes are by people that the child knows and you’re asking a child to then testify against a relative and try to get them executed," he said.
